ДЖН1-LANGUAGE WORD & RULE BOOK v6.63.927
========================================================================================

LANGUAGE CONCEPT
=======================================================================================
DXN1-Language is an English-first conlang written mostly in Cyrillic.
It is not Russian, not a translation of Russian, and not a literal cipher.
Its job is to keep English meaning readable while making the text look coded, stylized, and fun.
Core idea:
- English grammar stays mostly readable.
- Cyrillic gives the language its visual identity.
- Mixed-script forms are allowed on purpose.
- Short forms and slang are part of the language, not mistakes.
- The system grows by roots, affixes, and borrowed terms.
CREATOR & ORIGIN
Creator: Dani Postma
DXN1-Language was created by Dani Postma as an English-first, Cyrillic-written,
stylized conlang for texting, gaming, secret notes, slang, and creative worldbuilding.
MODES
Casual: fast texting, short, readable, loose spelling.
Standard: the default clean dictionary form.
Hard: compressed, mixed-script, more coded, harder to skim.
Nightmare: extra compressed, symbolic, and intentionally messy.
READING RULE
If someone knows English, they should be able to guess the meaning.
If someone does not know English, the text should feel like a secret system.
DXN1 uses Cyrillic for the body of the language, but Latin letters may appear in names, brands, tech terms, emphasis, and hard mode.
SOUND STYLE
The language likes clean consonant beats, short vowels, repeated letters for emotion, clipped gamer-text energy, and a sharp futuristic feel.
GRAMMAR ENGINES
1) Root words stay stable.
2) Tense is marked mostly by helper particles.
3) Negation stays simple.
4) Questions use question particles or word order.
5) New words are built from roots plus DXN1 suffixes.
6) Slang can compress the word whenever the meaning is still clear.
TENSE & ASPECT MARKERS
был = past marker
буд = future marker
из = continuous / ongoing
ду = completed / perfect
не = negation
ли = question marker
же = emphasis / obviousness
то = topic / contrast marker
ка = casual filler / vibe marker
ну = hesitation / softening marker
ORTHOGRAPHY & STYLE
- Use Cyrillic as the main body script.
- Use Latin letters for names, URLs, brands, coding terms, and emphasis.
- Keep English word order unless a DXN1 marker changes it.
- Keep contractions short when texting.
- Repeat letters for emotion: сооо, даа, нээт, лолл.
- One word can have 3 faces: casual, standard, and hard.
GRAMMAR RULES
Noun structure: singular is the base root. Plural uses -s / -z / -и / -ы depending on style.
Ownership can use my/your/our markers or possessive suffixes.
Verb structure: root stays stable. Tense is marked by helper particles.
Aspect markers can stack. Negation stays before the verb. Questions can use ли, intonation, or a question word.
Default sentence skeleton: subject + tense/aspect + verb + object + place + mood marker.
Examples: я был ид дом = I went home; мы из говор музик = we are speaking about music; ю не лайк это = you do not like this.

OPERATING NOTES
- The dictionary can keep growing by category without breaking the system.
- New slang should follow the same visual rhythm.
- Mixed-script spelling is a feature, not an error.
- The language is built for speed, identity, and secrecy.
- A user should be able to write casual chat quickly and then upgrade to hard mode for style.

SLUR-LIKE DESIGN RULES
- DXN1 can have harsh insults, but they should be invented words, not real-world hate slurs.
- Insults can target behavior, attitude, energy, ego, skill, or chaos.
- Avoid targeting protected groups.
- You can intensify a word by adding: очень, супер, ультра, мрак, или пусто.
- You can soften a word by adding: немного, почти, or basically context.
- For friend-to-friend trash talk, use mild terms first; reserve harsh ones for dramatic moments.
INSULT GRAMMAR
X + рот = loudmouth / annoying talker
X + мозг = type of mind / mental vibe
X + вайб = mood or energy label
X + код = mode or identity
X + фейс = visible style or face-energy
X + шаг = movement / action style
X + чат = chat behavior
X + режим = operating mode

PRODUCTIVE FORM RULES
Most new words can grow into families:
- noun/base form
- verb form: add -ить / -нуть / -ать
- adjective form: add -ный / -овой / -истый
- person form: add -ер / -щик / -ник
- place form: add -дом / -лог / -зон / -блок
- anti-form: add анти-
- mega-form: add мега-
- broken/unstable form: add крив- or глитч-

SLANG GROWTH RULES
- Add -ка for casual object names: чатка, лобка, лагка.
- Add -ик for smaller or cuter tone: кодик, глитчик, вайбик.
- Add -ища for huge or intense tone: лагище, драмища, крашища.
- Add -нуть for quick action: кликнуть, пингнуть, крашнуть.
- Add анти- for counter / reverse / anti-mode.
- Add мега- for extremely strong form.
- Add крив- for broken or unstable form.
- Add фейк- for fake versions.
- Add хард- for serious mode.
- Add лайт- for softer mode.

GENDER SYSTEM
DXN1-Language marks grammatical gender with a light prefix system, not full agreement.
This is optional flavor grammar — Standard mode can skip it, Hard/Nightmare modes use it more.
Default / masculine (no prefix, base form):
мй - my (default/masc) | хй - his-flavored "my" | хе - he (unchanged core)
Feminine (prefix ф-):
фмй - my (fem-flavored, "my" said/used by or about a female) | Meaning: моя (fem) | Type: gender
фхэр - her (fem-marked possessive, emphatic) | Meaning: её (fem, emphatic) | Type: gender
фше - she (fem-marked, emphatic form of ше) | Meaning: она (emphatic) | Type: gender
фхи - girl/female person marker, standalone | Meaning: женщина/девушка-маркер | Type: gender
Neutral / unspecified (prefix н-):
нмй - my (neutral, gender unspecified or not relevant) | Meaning: моё (neutral) | Type: gender
нит - it/they-singular neutral marker | Meaning: оно/они (neutral singular) | Type: gender
RULE: ф- = feminine flavor, н- = neutral/unspecified flavor, no prefix = default/masc-neutral.
This prefix can attach to most possessives and pronoun-adjacent words when the speaker wants
to be explicit about gender (мй → фмй → нмй), but base forms remain gender-neutral by default,
matching the "reading rule" that DXN1 stays readable and low-friction in Standard/Casual mode.
Examples:
мй кар - my car (default/neutral).
фмй кар - my car (said in a feminine-marked way, e.g. a girl emphasizing "my").
хй бро сэйд фхэр стори агейн - his bro said her story again (fem-marked "her").
нмй динер, нит чойс - my dinner (neutral), their/its choice (neutral marker).
DIFFICULTY LEVELS (A1–C2) — EXPANDED CEFR SYSTEM (v5.9)
DXN1-Language follows a full CEFR-style curve, now split into sub-levels (.1/.2) so
learners can track granular progress the way real-language learners do. Each level lists:
core grammar unlocked, vocabulary scope, a mastery checklist, and worked examples.
A1.1 — First contact:
Grammar: default sentence skeleton (subject + verb + object) only. No tense marking —
present tense is assumed by context. No negation, no questions yet.
Vocab: core pronouns (и, йау, хе, ше, ит, ве, зей), core verbs (бе, хаве, до, лайк, ноу),
greetings (хей, йо, сап), numbers 0-10.
Mastery checklist: can name self and others, can say "I like/want X," can count 0-10.
Example: и лайк фуд - I like food. | ит из мй кар - it is my car.
A1.2 — Basic expansion:
Grammar: negation with не (before the verb, RC/TR rules not required yet — treat as fixed
phrase не + verb). Simple yes/no questions with ли.
Vocab: family, home, food, and body words; numbers 11-100 (teens, tens, hundred).
Mastery checklist: can negate a simple sentence, can ask/answer yes-no questions, can
count to 100 and give an age or a simple price.
Example: и не лайк зис - I do not like this. | ю лайк музик ли? - do you like music?
A2.1 — Everyday basics:
Grammar: tense markers был (past) and буд (future) attach directly before the verb.
Vocab: daily life words (work, home, food, family, weather), days of the week, clock time
(оклок, хаф паст, квортер ту).
Mastery checklist: can narrate a simple past or future event, can state clock time,
can describe a daily routine in 3-4 linked sentences.
Example: и был ат ворк тудей - I was at work today. | и буд гоу тумороу - I will go tomorrow.
A2.2 — Everyday fluency:
Grammar: quantity words (сам, мени, фью, ол) and basic ordinals (фёрст-тенф) in normal
sentences; simple comparative descriptions using adjectives without special morphology.
Vocab: shopping, transport, hobbies, weather, feelings (basic tier).
Mastery checklist: can shop/order using quantity words, can give a simple ordered list
using ordinals, can describe feelings in one clause.
Example: и хаве мени френдс - I have many friends. | зис из мй фёрст тайм хир - this is my first time here.
B1.1 — Independent use:
Grammar: aspect markers (из = continuous, ду = completed) stack after tense markers per
TR2-TR4; casual filler particles (ка, ну) start appearing for tone softening.
Vocab: event/situation words (хаппенд, ситуейшн, стори), emotions (medium tier), school
and work vocabulary.
Mastery checklist: can describe an ongoing action vs. a completed one in the same
paragraph, can soften a statement with ну, can tell a short two-event story.
Example: и из зинк эбаут зат синг зат хаппенд - I'm thinking about that thing that happened.
B1.2 — Independent fluency:
Grammar: role/case marking basics (RC1-RC5): unmarked SVO subjects, particle-marked
objects when ambiguity is possible, basic locative particles for place.
Vocab: travel, tech/digital words, expanded body & health vocabulary.
Mastery checklist: can disambiguate subject/object in a two-noun sentence, can describe
a trip or a tech problem, can hold a 5+ sentence conversation without switching to English.
Example: и гив зе бук ту хим ин зе хаус - I give the book to him in the house.
B2.1 — Fluency building:
Grammar: full word-building kit (prefixes ре-/анти-/мега-/etc. + suffixes -ер/-инг/-мод/
etc.) becomes productive; verb conjugation classes (VC1-VC6) apply consistently.
Vocab: productive families (глитч → глитчить → глитчный → глитчер), gaming/tech slang,
Empire Foods culture words.
Mastery checklist: can coin a new word on the spot using a known prefix/suffix and have
it be understood, can sort a verb into its conjugation class correctly.
Example: зе системс глитчнуть агейн - the systems glitched again.
B2.2 — Fluency with texture:
Grammar: gender-marking system (GA1-GA10) used naturally but optionally; Hard-mode vowel
compression (PH1-PH10) readable at conversational speed.
Vocab: masculine/feminine wording set, profanity Low/Medium tier, extended daily-life
batches.
Mastery checklist: can read a Hard-mode sentence aloud without stalling, can mark gender
correctly per GA3/GA4 when it matters, can use Low-tier profanity appropriately.
Example: фстронг ше из, бат хе стил трайинг - she's strong (fem-marked), but he's still trying.
C1.1 — Advanced use:
Grammar: full profanity register (Low/Hard/Very Harsh, per WR9), syntax constraint rules
(SX1-SX12) enforced, topic/emphasis particles (же, то) used deliberately for tone control.
Vocab: harsh-tier slang, idiomatic slang stacking, advanced connectors (энд, бат).
Mastery checklist: can escalate or de-escalate register mid-conversation on purpose,
can use же/то to redirect emphasis without changing word order.
Example: зис же зат пиздец синг агейн, но ксар зат - this is THAT disaster thing again, but screw it.
C1.2 — Advanced fluency:
Grammar: mixed-script Hard mode read and produced fluently; register/dialect rules
(RD1-RD9) understood well enough to code-switch mode mid-document intentionally.
Vocab: Very Harsh profanity tier, coded/secret-note vocabulary, full numeric system
including fractions and negative numbers.
Mastery checklist: can write a coded Hard-mode note that a fellow C1+ speaker can parse
but an A-level learner cannot, can explain the difference between register and dialect.
Example: не-фифтин дигриз ауцайд, бат ве стил гоуин - negative fifteen degrees outside, but we're still going.
C2.1 — Native-like range:
Grammar: Nightmare mode (extra-compressed, symbolic, intentionally messy) produced and
parsed reliably; full command of every rule section (A-K).
Vocab: full lexicon across all registers, all profanity tiers, all culture-word families.
Mastery checklist: can freely invent new productive-form words on the fly per the
word-building kit and have them parse correctly under WR1-WR12.
Example: нау-хпнд, зхпнд, фмй сит же кривсук — ксар ол, ве раун агейн.
(now-it-happened, that happened, my situation [fem] is a twisted-snake mess — screw it all, we go again.)
C2.2 — Native-like mastery:
Grammar: fluid mid-sentence switching between Casual/Standard/Hard/Nightmare per RD2
while respecting SX1-SX12 clause-by-clause; full pragmatic command of tone, dialect,
and coded register simultaneously.
Vocab: no ceiling — this is the level at which the speaker is expected to coin, not
just use, DXN1 vocabulary, and to teach lower levels.
Mastery checklist: can hold a full conversation entirely in Nightmare mode with another
C2 speaker, can explain and teach any rule in Sections A-K to a lower-level learner.
LEVEL-TO-MODE MAPPING
A1-A2 → Standard mode only.
B1-B2 → Standard + Casual mode, light Hard mode exposure.
C1 → Casual + Hard mode fluency.
C2 → Full fluency across Casual, Standard, Hard, and Nightmare modes.
MORE VERBS (v5.3)
connect - коннект | Meaning: соедини | Casual: коннект | Hard: кнкт | Type: verb
call (v) - колл | Meaning: звони | Casual: колл | Hard: колл | Type: verb
repair - рипейр | Meaning: почини | Casual: рипейр | Hard: рпр | Type: verb
kind (adj) - кайнд | Meaning: добрый | Casual: кайнд | Hard: кнд | Type: adjective
Verb families follow the same productive rules: root + -ить/-нуть/-ать for extra forms
where useful, e.g. траст → трастить (to trust, ongoing), форгет → форгетнуть (to forget, once).
MASCULINE / FEMININE WORDING SYSTEM (v5.3)
This expands the v5.2 gender prefixes (ф-/н-) into a light word-ending agreement system
for adjectives, descriptive words, and some nouns. Still optional flavor grammar — Standard
mode can ignore it, Hard/Nightmare mode leans on it for extra texture.
RULE:
- Masculine ending: -ов / -ер / base form (no change) — e.g. стронг (strong, masc/default)
- Feminine ending: -ова / -ка / ф- prefix — e.g. фстронг or стронгова (strong, fem-marked)
- Neutral/plural ending: -о / -и — e.g. стронго (strong, neutral/general)
This mirrors natural gendered languages (like Russian -ов/-ова endings) but stays lightweight:
you only mark gender when it matters for the sentence, not on every word.
MASCULINE WORDING EXAMPLES:
стронгер - strong one (masc) | лкий - lucky one (masc, from лаки) | смартов - smart one (masc)
кайндер - kind one (masc) | бравев - brave one (masc)
FEMININE WORDING EXAMPLES:
фстронг / стронгова - strong one (fem) | флаки / лакова - lucky one (fem) | фсмарт / смартова - smart one (fem)
факайнд / кайндова - kind one (fem) | фбраве / бравева - brave one (fem)
NEUTRAL / GROUP WORDING EXAMPLES:
стронго - strong (neutral/plural) | лакио - lucky (neutral/plural) | смарто - smart (neutral/plural)
USAGE:
хе из стронгер - he is strong (masc-marked).
ше из фстронг / стронгова - she is strong (fem-marked).
зей ар стронго - they are strong (neutral/plural).
мй бро из смартов, мй систер из фсмарт - my brother is smart, my sister is smart (fem).
This system is fully optional — DXN1 sentences work fine with zero gender marking at all
(base adjective form is gender-neutral by default), this just adds a way to flavor it in.
ADVANCED RULESET (v5.4)
This section formalizes strict rule numbering for gender agreement, wording construction,
and time marking. These rules govern Hard and Nightmare mode output; Standard and Casual
mode may relax or skip any rule below without violating the language.
SECTION A — GENDER AGREEMENT RULES (GA1–GA14)
GA1. Every noun or pronoun referring to a person may carry a gender marker; objects,
     abstractions, and unknown-gender referents default to unmarked (masc/neutral) form.
GA2. Masculine marking is the null marker: absence of ф- or н- on a markable word IS the
     masculine/default reading. There is no separate masculine prefix; zero-marking = masc.
GA3. Feminine marking is prefix ф- attached directly to the root with no space and no
     hyphen: фмй, фхэр, фстронг, фсмарт. The prefix never attaches to particles (был, буд,
     не, ли, же, то, ка, ну) or to function words (зе, а, ан).
GA4. Neutral/unspecified marking is prefix н- and is used only when gender is genuinely
     unknown, irrelevant, or the referent is non-human/plural-mixed. Do not use н- as a
     substitute for ф- to soften or avoid marking feminine gender.
GA5. Gender marking on a possessive (мй → фмй) does not automatically change the gender
     marking on the noun it modifies; each markable word carries its own marker
     independently. Full-sentence agreement is optional style, not a requirement.
GA6. When a sentence contains two different gendered referents, each referent's marker
     applies only to words directly describing that referent, never to shared verbs,
     particles, or tense/aspect markers, which stay unmarked at all times.
GA7. A word may only carry one gender marker at a time. Stacking ф- and н- on the same
     root (e.g. фнмй) is invalid and must not be produced.
GA8. Suffix-based feminine forms (-ова, -ка) are reserved for adjective/descriptive roots
     already ending in a consonant cluster compatible with the suffix; when the root ends
     in a vowel or soft cluster, the ф- prefix form is used instead of the suffix form.
GA9. Reduplicated or repeated-letter emotional forms (сооо, даа) do not take gender
     marking; emotional intensity markers sit outside the gender system entirely.
GA10. In Nightmare mode, gender marking may be compressed to a single leading ligature
      character where legible, but must still be recoverable to ф- or н- on inspection.
GA11. Compound titles/roles (e.g. team-lead, co-founder) take gender marking on the head
      noun only, never on both halves of the compound: фтим-лид, not фтим-флид.
GA12. When a speaker refers to themselves, self-applied gender marking is always optional
      and never required, even in Hard/Nightmare mode — GA1's markability rule applies to
      third-person and second-person referents by default, first-person by choice only.
GA13. A gender marker applied to a group noun (тим, скваад, крю) marks the group's
      perceived collective gender identity, not the gender of any individual member;
      mixed-gender groups default to unmarked per GA2 unless the speaker deliberately
      chooses to mark the group as a whole.
GA14. Gender marking never attaches to numerals, ordinals, or quantity words (Section K);
      "three of them, fem-marked" marks the pronoun зей, not the numeral фри.
SECTION B — WORDING CONSTRUCTION RULES (WR1–WR16)
WR1. Base root order is fixed: [gender marker] + [root] + [productive suffix]. No other
     ordering is valid; suffixes never precede the root, gender markers never follow it.
WR2. Only one productive suffix family (-ер/-щик/-ник for person; -ный/-овой/-истый for
     adjective; -ить/-нуть/-ать for verb) may attach per word. Do not chain two suffix
     families onto a single root in Standard or Casual mode.
WR3. In Hard mode, a second suffix family may chain onto the first only if the resulting
     word remains parseable back to its root within two strip operations.
WR4. Compound words formed from two roots (e.g. холтскат, крайдрит) place the modifying
     root first and the head root second, matching English-order compounding, not
     Russian-order compounding.
WR5. When attaching -ов/-ова/-о gender-agreement endings to a word that already carries a
     productive suffix, the gender ending replaces the final vowel of the suffix rather
     than stacking after it (e.g. стронгер + fem → стронгера, not стронгерова).
WR6. Prefix builders (ре-, ун-, но-, анти-, гипер-, мега-, микро-, нео-, прото-, гост-,
     глитч-, хард-, софт-, турбо-, дарк-, брайт-) attach directly to the root with no
     space; gender markers, if present, sit between the prefix builder and the root:
     мега + ф + стронг → мегафстронг, never фмегастронг.
WR7. A word carrying both a prefix builder and a suffix family must resolve the prefix
     builder first, then the root, then the suffix family, in that fixed order, with any
     gender marker inserted per WR6.
WR8. Slang compression (dropping vowels, e.g. смарт → смрт) may only occur in Hard or
     Nightmare mode and may never delete a gender marker (ф-/н-) or a tense/aspect
     particle, only interior root vowels.
WR9. When two profanity-tier roots are compounded (Very Harsh tier), the harsher root is
     placed second, matching intensifier-last ordering already used in existing forms
     (морграх, кривсрак, злобрак).
WR10. Loanword/tech roots (глитч, хак, краш, лаг) follow the standard productive suffix
      rules exactly as native roots; no separate rule set exists for loanwords.
WR11. A newly coined word is only valid if it can take at minimum one productive suffix
      form (verb, adjective, or person) without violating WR1–WR10.
WR12. Casual-mode contractions (зкс, тй, нп) are exempt from WR1–WR11 entirely; they are
      frozen forms and may not be further inflected, gendered, or suffixed.
WR13. A root may only carry one productive prefix at a time; stacking two builders
      (e.g. мега- + турбо- on one root) requires a hyphen and is treated as a compound,
      not a single derived word — мега-турбокар, not мегатурбокар.
WR14. Suffix -макс and prefix мега- may not co-occur on the same root, since both mark
      maximum intensity; use one or the other, never both (redundant-intensity block).
WR15. A coined word's stress/emphasis (marked by repeated final letter per orthography
      rules) attaches after all suffixes are applied, never between root and suffix.
WR16. When two existing roots are compounded into a new culture-word (per the Empire
      Foods model), the resulting compound is treated as a single frozen lexical item and
      does not itself take further prefixes or suffixes — coin a new word instead of
      stacking onto a compound.
SECTION C — TIME RULES (TR1–TR15)
TR1. Tense marking is mandatory in Standard mode for any verb describing an action
     outside the immediate present; был (past) or буд (future) must appear before the verb.
TR2. Present tense carries zero marker; the unmarked verb form IS present tense by default,
     exactly mirroring GA2's zero-marking convention for masculine/default gender.
TR3. Aspect markers (из = continuous, ду = completed/perfect) may stack with a tense
     marker in fixed order: [tense marker] + [aspect marker] + [verb]. Aspect never
     precedes tense.
TR4. Only one tense marker may appear per clause. был and буд never co-occur in the same
     clause; a sentence needing both past and future reference requires two clauses.
TR5. Only one aspect marker may appear per verb. из and ду never stack directly on the
     same verb; if both continuous and completed meaning are needed, use two verbs.
TR6. Time-word modifiers (нау/ноу, зен, тудей/тодэй, тумороу/томорроу, естедей/йестэрдэй,
     латэр, сун, олреди/алридй, стилл, агейн, агоу) are placed after the tense/aspect
     block and before the object, never before the subject.
TR7. ago (агоу) requires an explicit duration or reference point in the same clause;
     it cannot stand alone as a bare time marker the way нау or зен can.
TR8. already (алридй) and still (стилл) are mutually exclusive within a single clause;
     they encode opposite completion states and must not co-occur on one verb.
TR9. Event/reference words (хаппенд, ситуейшн, стори, момент, дил) default to past tense
     reading when used without an explicit tense marker, since they inherently describe
     completed or ongoing situations rather than present actions.
TR10. When a time word and a tense marker would conflict (e.g. нау with был), the explicit
      time word overrides the tense marker's default reading; ноу был синг = "it was a
      now-thing" (past framing of a present-tense event), not a grammatical error.
TR11. Question marker ли, when combined with a time word, is placed immediately after the
      time word and before the verb: зен ли ю но? (did you know, back then?).
TR12. Duration is expressed with фор + time-length placed after the verb phrase: и вейт
      фор ту ауэрс = I waited for two hours. фор is never used for a point-in-time.
TR13. "Since" (a starting point continuing to now) uses синс + time word, and pairs
      naturally with continuous aspect из: и из ворк синс морнинг = I've been working
      since morning.
TR14. Sequential time ("first... then... after that") uses фёрст, зен, and афтер зат as
      fixed connective time words; they may open a clause but never combine with each
      other in the same clause head.
TR15. When no time word or tense marker is present at all, the default reading is present
      tense per TR2 — but this default is overridden the moment ANY time word (нau, зен,
      тумороу, etc.) appears anywhere in the clause, even without a formal tense marker.
SECTION D — ROLE / CASE MARKING RULES (RC1–RC17)
DXN1-Language does not use full noun-case declension, but marks grammatical role through
a fixed set of postposed particles when word order alone would be ambiguous.
RC1. Subject role carries zero marker in unambiguous SVO order; explicit subject marking
     is never required when the subject precedes the verb.
RC2. Direct object role, when the object could otherwise be mistaken for a second subject
     (e.g. two animate nouns in one clause), takes the postposed particle то directly
     after the object noun: хе си врек то (he sees the fuck-up [object]).
RC3. Indirect object / recipient role takes the postposed particle фор (borrowed function
     word, not a full preposition system) placed between the direct object and the
     recipient: и гив дил фор хим (I give the deal to him).
RC4. Instrumental role (the thing something is done "with") takes postposed particle виз
     placed immediately after the instrument noun: хе фикс ит виз тул (he fixes it
     with a tool).
RC5. Locative role (place where) takes postposed particle ин, ат, or он depending on
     containment (ин), point-location (ат), or surface (он); these are not
     interchangeable and follow English locative logic, not Russian case logic.
RC6. Genitive/possessive role outside the core possessive pronouns (мй, хис, хэр, etc.)
     is marked by placing the possessor noun before the possessed noun with no linking
     particle, mirroring English "noun noun" compounding: врек мани (the fuck-up's money).
RC7. Vocative role (direct address) is marked by placing the addressed noun at the
     absolute start or end of the clause, set off by comma in written form: брах, зис
     хаппенд or зис хаппенд, брах — both valid, meaning shifts emphasis only.
RC8. When RC2 (object marker то) and the topic marker то (from the core particle table)
     would collide in the same clause, the object-role то is dropped and word order alone
     disambiguates; the language never stacks two functionally different то in one clause.
RC9. Role particles (то, фор, виз, ин/ат/он) never take gender marking, tense marking,
     or productive suffixes; they are invariant function words.
RC10. A clause may contain at most one instrumental (виз) and one locative (ин/ат/он)
     particle; stacking two locatives requires two clauses.
RC11. Pronoun objects (him, her, it, them, us — see object pronoun table) already encode
     object role morphologically and never additionally take particle то.
RC12. In Hard mode, role particles may cliticize onto the preceding word with no space
     (e.g. хэрфор) provided the resulting form does not collide with an existing lexeme;
     if collision would occur, the particle must remain a separate word.
RC13. Nightmare mode may drop role particles entirely when context makes role recoverable
     from real-world plausibility alone; this is the only rule set that permits full
     omission of an otherwise-required marker.
RC14. The instrumental particle виз ("with") is distinct from the accompaniment sense of
      "with" (a person doing something together with you) — accompaniment instead uses
      the connector энд or a shared-subject construction, never виз.
RC15. Benefactive role ("for the benefit of") uses фор and is not interchangeable with
      the directional/goal sense of фор seen in TR12's duration marking; context (a
      person vs. a duration) disambiguates which фор is meant.
RC16. When a sentence has three or more role-marked constituents (subject, object,
      location, instrument), Standard mode strongly prefers splitting into two clauses;
      only Hard/Nightmare mode permits a single clause with 3+ role particles stacked.
RC17. A reflexive object (myself, himself — see reflexive pronoun table) blocks the
      object-role particle то entirely; reflexives are self-marking and редундант particle
      use is invalid: хе хёрт химсэлф, not хе хёрт то химсэлф.
SECTION E — VERB CONJUGATION CLASS RULES (VC1–VC18)
Verbs sort into three conjugation classes based on root ending. Class determines which
allomorph of the productive suffix family attaches.
VC1. Class I (consonant-final roots: бе, хаве, до, ливе, коннект): take -ить for the
     ongoing/infinitive-adjacent form and -ил for the simple completed form.
VC2. Class II (vowel-final roots: чуз, си, трв): take -ить minus the linking vowel,
     producing -ть directly on the root, and -л for the completed form.
VC3. Class III (borrowed/tech roots ending in a hard consonant cluster: глитч, краш,
     хак): take -нуть for the punctual/single-event form in addition to the standard
     -ить ongoing form; Class I and II roots do not take -нуть unless explicitly listed
     as dual-class in the lexicon (e.g. форгет is Class I but also permits форгетнуть).
VC4. Every verb has exactly one conjugation class; class is fixed at coinage and does
     not change based on mode (Casual/Standard/Hard/Nightmare).
VC5. The imperative form removes all tense/aspect marking and uses the bare root with
     rising intonation (written) or an exclamation mark: лив! (leave!).
VC6. The negative imperative places не directly before the bare root with no tense
     marker: не лив (don't leave) — не буд лив is a future prohibition, a distinct
     and separately valid construction, not an error variant of the simple negative.
VC7. Reflexive meaning (doing something to oneself) is marked by repeating the subject
     pronoun immediately after the verb rather than by a bound reflexive suffix: хе си хе
     (he sees himself), not a special reflexive verb form.
VC8. Causative meaning (making something happen) is marked by placing мк (from маке, see
     core verb table) before the second verb in its bare root form: и мк хим лив (I make
     him leave).
VC9. Passive-like meaning is constructed periphrastically with бе + past participle
     analog (verb root + -ед), never with a dedicated passive suffix: ит бе брикед (it is
     broken/gets broken).
VC10. Modal meaning (can/must/should) is expressed by a small closed set of modal
      particles placed directly before the bare verb root, which itself takes no further
      tense marking while under a modal: кэн (can), маст (must), шуд (should).
VC11. When a modal particle is present, tense is marked on the modal itself, not on the
      main verb: и был маст лив (I had to leave), never и маст был лив.
VC12. Serial verb constructions (two verbs describing one continuous event) place both
      verbs back-to-back with no connector, aspect marked once on the first verb only:
      хе из ран джамп (he is running-jumping, one fluid action).
VC13. Verb + particle phrasal combinations (existing forms like ксар оф "fuck off") are
      lexicalized units; the particle in these combinations is frozen and cannot be
      separated, reordered, or independently negated.
VC14. Aspectual reduplication (repeating the bare root twice with no space) marks
      habitual/repeated action distinct from из (continuous-in-progress): ранран =
      "runs regularly / keeps running as a habit," versus из ран = "is running right now."
VC15. Class III (loanword/tech roots ending in a cluster: глитч, краш, лаг) take -нуть
      exclusively for the punctual/one-time verb form; they never take -ить, which is
      reserved for Class I roots per VC1.
VC16. A verb's conjugation class is fixed at coinage and does not change if the word
      later gains new suffixed forms; a Class II root stays Class II across every
      derived form built from it.
VC17. Imperative forms (per MM8) are exempt from conjugation-class marking entirely —
      the bare root is used regardless of class, since imperatives carry no tense/aspect.
VC18. When a verb is borrowed directly from a nightmare-tier coinage (Section on Nightmare
      Words), its conjugation class defaults to Class III unless the root's final sound
      clearly matches Class I or II per VC1–VC2's phonetic criteria.
SECTION F — SYNTAX & WORD ORDER CONSTRAINT RULES (SX1–SX16)
SX1. Default clause order is strict SVO (subject-verb-object); deviation is only valid
     for topic-fronting (marked by то) or vocative placement (RC7).
SX2. Adjectives precede the noun they modify, matching English order, never following it
     as in Russian postposed-adjective poetic constructions.
SX3. Adverbs of manner follow the verb they modify; adverbs of time follow TR6's
     placement rule (after tense/aspect block, before object).
SX4. Question particle ли attaches at clause-final position by default; front-position ли
     (clause-initial) is reserved for Hard/Nightmare mode emphatic questions only.
SX5. Negation particle не always immediately precedes the element being negated, not
     necessarily the verb: не хе лив (it's not HIM who left) negates the subject, while
     хе не лив (he did not leave) negates the verb.
SX6. Emphasis particle же attaches directly after the emphasized word, never at clause
     boundary, and may only emphasize one element per clause.
SX7. Coordination of two clauses uses энд (and) or бат (but) as invariant connectors
     placed between the clauses with no comma required in Casual mode, comma required in
     Standard mode.
SX8. Subordinate clauses (because, if, when) are introduced by a fixed subordinator set
     (кос = because, иф = if, вен = when) placed at the start of the subordinate clause,
     which may precede or follow the main clause with no meaning change.
SX9. Relative clauses (the thing that...) use зат as both the demonstrative and the
     relativizer; DXN1 does not have a separate relative pronoun, disambiguation is by
     position only.
SX10. Multiple adjectives stacking before one noun follow size-then-quality-then-origin
      ordering when order matters for clarity, but free ordering is permitted in Casual
      mode where clarity is not at stake.
SX11. Ellipsis (dropping a repeated subject or verb across coordinated clauses) is
      permitted only in Casual and Hard mode; Standard mode requires the subject or verb
      to be restated in the second clause.
SX12. A well-formed DXN1 sentence in Standard mode must satisfy SX1, TR1–TR2 (tense
      marking), and GA1–GA2 (gender defaulting) simultaneously; failing any one of these
      three does not produce ungrammaticality in Casual/Hard/Nightmare mode, only in
      Standard mode, which is the strictest register.
SX13. Subordinate clauses (introduced by зат "that," иф "if," or a time connector from
      TR14) follow the main clause by default; fronting the subordinate clause for
      emphasis is permitted only in Casual, Hard, and Nightmare mode.
SX14. Question words (ху "who," вот "what," вен "when," вер "where," вай "why," хау
      "how") move to clause-initial position, displacing the default SVO order — this is
      the one context where SX1's fixed order is overridden without penalty.
SX15. Negation particle не always attaches immediately before the element it negates,
      not automatically before the verb — не мени = "not many" negates the quantity word,
      while и не гоу negates the verb; scope is local to whatever не directly precedes.
SX16. A single clause may contain at most one modal (per MM6), one aspect marker, and
      one tense marker; a clause attempting to combine more than this maximum must be
      split into two clauses joined by энд/бат per DC3's short-clause preference.
SECTION G — PHONOLOGICAL & ORTHOGRAPHIC RULES (PH1–PH14)
PH1. Consonant clusters longer than three consonants in a row are broken with an epenthetic
     ъ in Standard mode (never in Hard/Nightmare, where clusters are preserved for
     compression); e.g. a coined strongstr root becomes стронгъстр in Standard mode.
PH2. Stress falls on the root syllable by default; prefixes and suffixes are never
     stressed except in emphatic/shouted forms (repeated-letter forms per PH4).
PH3. Vowel length is not phonemic; doubled vowels in writing (сооо, даа, нээт) mark
     emotional intensity, not a distinct long-vowel phoneme.
PH4. Repeated final consonant (лолл, нээт) marks emphasis and may combine with repeated
     vowels for maximum intensity (лоооллл), with no formal upper limit but a practical
     three-repeat convention in Standard-register writing.
PH5. Latin letters embedded in a Cyrillic sentence (for brand names, tech terms, URLs) do
     not take DXN1 productive suffixes directly; a Latin loanword must first be
     transliterated into Cyrillic before it can be inflected (e.g. "Discord" becomes
     дискорд before taking -ить).
PH6. Hard-mode vowel deletion (WR8) may not delete a vowel that is the sole vowel in a
     monosyllabic root, since this would produce an unpronounceable form; ит, зе, зен are
     immune to Hard-mode compression for this reason.
PH7. Word-final devoicing (voiced consonants becoming voiceless at the end of a word) is
     NOT a feature of DXN1-Language, unlike Russian; врек is always pronounced with a
     voiced к-adjacent cluster reading, not devoiced.
PH8. Capitalization is not grammatically meaningful in DXN1; it is used only for names,
     sentence-initial position in Standard mode, and emphasis in any mode, never to mark
     case or gender.
PH9. Punctuation follows English conventions (period, comma, question mark, exclamation
     mark) rather than any DXN1-specific punctuation system; no new punctuation marks are
     introduced by this or any prior expansion pack.
PH10. When transliterating a new loanword, the closest Cyrillic phonetic match is always
      preferred over a literal letter-for-letter substitution; this is why "shower"
      becomes шоуэр and not a mechanical transliteration of the English spelling.
PH11. Hard-mode vowel compression (dropping unstressed vowels) never drops the first
      vowel of a root, since that vowel typically carries the sound that makes the root
      recognizable; трст (trust) keeps none, but names and greetings are exempt entirely.
PH12. Consonant clusters created by compression must remain pronounceable in at least
      one plausible reading; a compression that produces an unpronounceable cluster
      reverts to Casual-mode spelling instead of Hard mode for that word.
PH13. Latin-letter emphasis (per the orthography rules) is reserved for brand names,
      tech terms, and deliberate code-switch emphasis — it is never used to Latinize an
      ordinary Cyrillic-spelled DXN1 root just for stylistic flair.
PH14. Nightmare-mode symbolic compression (replacing letters with numerals or symbols,
      e.g. 3 for з) is permitted only on roots already established in Standard mode;
      brand-new coinages must debut in full Cyrillic spelling before earning a symbolic form.
SECTION H — REGISTER & DIALECT RULES (RD1–RD13)
RD1. The four modes (Casual, Standard, Hard, Nightmare) are registers, not dialects; a
     single speaker moves between them based on context, not regional or social identity.
RD2. Switching modes mid-sentence (permitted at C2 level per the difficulty-level mapping)
     must still respect SX1–SX12 within whichever mode governs the clause currently being
     produced.
RD3. Profanity-tier vocabulary (Low/Hard/Very Harsh) is independent of register mode; Low
     harsh profanity may appear in Casual mode, Very Harsh profanity may appear in
     Standard mode if the content calls for it — tier and register are orthogonal axes.
RD4. A "dialect" in DXN1 terms refers to a consistent personal or community pattern of
     which optional rules (gender marking, role particles, aspectual reduplication) a
     speaker chooses to use habitually; dialects do not violate the core ruleset, they
     select from its optional branches consistently.
RD5. No dialect may omit TR1 (mandatory tense marking) in Standard-register writing, as
     this is a core-grammar rule rather than an optional stylistic branch.
RD6. Texting/gaming register (the original design target per the CREATOR & ORIGIN section)
     defaults to Casual mode rules unless the context is a formal in-game announcement or
     document, which defaults to Standard mode.
RD7. Secret-note / coded register defaults to Hard or Nightmare mode specifically because
     PH1, WR8, and RC13 all increase opacity to non-learners while remaining internally
     rule-governed for fluent speakers.
RD8. Worldbuilding/creative register (fiction, lore text) may freely mix all four modes
     within a single document as a stylistic device, provided each individual sentence
     remains internally consistent per RD2.
RD9. No register or dialect may introduce a rule that contradicts Sections A–G; new
     vocabulary and new productive forms may be coined freely, but the grammatical engine
     itself (gender, wording, time, case, conjugation, syntax, phonology) is fixed across
     all registers and dialects.
RD10. Nightmare-tier culture words (Section: Nightmare Words) default to Hard or
      Nightmare register on coinage; using one in Standard mode is grammatical but reads
      as intentionally jarring, similar to slang appearing in a formal document.
RD11. A speaker may hold a "floor register" for an entire conversation (per RD4's dialect
      concept) while still dipping into a different mode for a single quoted line (per
      DC4's reported-speech rule) without that dip counting as a full register switch.
RD12. Register downshifting (Standard → Casual) mid-conversation signals informality or
      closeness; register upshifting (Casual → Standard) signals seriousness or distance
      — this pragmatic reading is conventional across all dialects per RD4.
RD13. Teaching register (used when a C2 speaker per the CEFR system explains a rule to a
      learner) defaults to Standard mode regardless of the surrounding conversation's
      register, so the explanation itself stays maximally readable.
SECTION I — MODALITY & MOOD RULES (MM1–MM14)
MM1. Ability/possibility is marked by inserting кан directly before the main verb, after
     any tense marker: и кан гоу = I can go, и был кан гоу = I was able to go.
MM2. Obligation/necessity is marked by мaст before the verb: ю маст сэй ит = you must say it.
     Weak obligation ("should") uses шуд in the same slot: ю шуд трай = you should try.
MM3. Permission-asking uses кан + ли together (кан...ли frames a yes/no permission
     question): кан и гоу ли? = can I go?
MM4. Hypothetical/conditional clauses are marked with иф at the clause head; the result
     clause optionally takes буд even when describing a present hypothetical, to keep the
     irrealis reading unambiguous: иф ю трай, ю буд вин = if you try, you would win.
MM5. Desire stronger than вант ("want") uses виш + фор: и виш фор пис = I wish for peace.
     This is a distinct lexical item from вант, not a derived form.
MM6. Modal particles (кан, маст, шуд) never stack more than one per clause; layering two
     modals (e.g. "must be able to") requires two clauses joined by энд or a subordinate
     clause, not a double modal slot.
MM7. Negating a modal negates the modal itself, not the main verb: и кан не гоу = I cannot
     go (ability negated), not "I can [not-go]" as a separate reading.
MM8. Imperative mood drops the subject entirely and uses the bare verb root: гоу! = go!
     сэй ит! = say it! Aspect/tense markers do not attach to imperatives.
MM9. Suggestion/"let's" mood uses лец + verb root: лец гоу = let's go. лец is invariant
     and does not conjugate or take tense marking.
MM10. Regret/should-have constructions combine шуд + был before the verb: ю шуд был ноу =
      you should have known. This is the only case where two modal-adjacent markers stack,
      because шуд+был forms one fixed compound mood marker, not two independent modals.
MM11. Certainty/inference ("must be," in the epistemic sense, not the obligation sense of
      маст) uses шуэр + би: ит шуэр би трю = it must be true. This is a distinct lexical
      slot from маст and the two are never interchangeable despite both translating "must."
MM12. Warning mood ("watch out that...") uses кэрфул + зат at the clause head: кэрфул зат
      ит брейкс = watch out, it might break. This mood implies possibility, not certainty.
MM13. Prohibition ("must not") negates маст directly per MM7's modal-negation rule, but
      has its own fixed reading as an outright ban rather than a simple negated obligation:
      ю маст не гоу = you must not go (forbidden), stronger than шуд не гоу (advised against).
MM14. Modal particles never take gender marking, aspect marking, or productive suffixes;
      like role particles (RC9), they are invariant function words across every register.
SECTION J — DISCOURSE & COHESION RULES (DC1–DC13)
DC1. Pronoun reference defaults to the most recently named matching-gender referent;
     ambiguous reference should be resolved with a repeated noun, not a pronoun, per the
     Reading Rule's guessability principle.
DC2. Topic-marker то (from the core particle list) may only mark one constituent per
     clause and typically appears on the element being contrasted or re-raised from
     earlier discourse, not on brand-new information.
DC3. Discourse connectors чейн together longer than two clauses using энд/бат are
     discouraged in Standard mode; Standard mode prefers short clauses linked across
     separate sentences for readability, matching the Reading Rule.
DC4. Reported speech uses сэй + зат to introduce a quoted or paraphrased clause: хе сэй
     зат хе из тайрд = he said that he's tired. Direct quotation may drop зат in Casual mode.
DC5. Discourse-level emphasis (highlighting an entire previous clause, not just one word)
     uses же placed clause-initially rather than word-adjacently: же, ит хаппенд = seriously,
     it happened — distinct from же's word-level use per the core particle table.
DC6. Continuation across turns (one speaker picking up where another left off) may drop
     the subject if it is recoverable from the prior turn, but tense/aspect markers must
     still be stated explicitly — ellipsis applies to subjects only, never to TR markers.
DC7. Politeness downgrading (softening a command into a request) adds плиз clause-finally
     or clause-initially: гив ит плиз = give it, please. плиз does not affect verb marking.
DC8. Filler particle ну (hesitation/softening) and casual filler ка (vibe marker) may not
     co-occur in the same clause; each softens differently and stacking them produces an
     unreadable tone per the Reading Rule.
DC9. A discourse may freely mix register per RD8, but pronoun reference (DC1) and topic
     marking (DC2) must stay consistent across the mixed-register stretch so meaning
     doesn't fracture across the mode switch.
DC10. Backchannel words (short listener responses like "mm," "right," "got it") do not
      count as a turn for pronoun-reference purposes (DC1); the referent tracking carries
      through the backchannel to the next full utterance unaffected.
DC11. When correcting a previous statement, the corrected element is marked with топик
      particle то even if it was not the original topic, since correction inherently
      re-raises the element as newly relevant discourse information.
DC12. A rhetorical question (one not expecting an answer) still takes question marker ли
      per normal question rules — DXN1 does not grammatically distinguish rhetorical from
      genuine questions; the distinction is entirely pragmatic/contextual.
DC13. Silence/non-response in a conversational thread is not itself markable in the
      grammar; any commentary on a silence (e.g. "they went quiet") must be stated as an
      ordinary descriptive clause, not a special discourse particle.
SECTION K — COMPOUNDING & NUMERIC INTEGRATION RULES (CN1–CN12)
CN1. Numbers integrate into the noun phrase before the noun, same slot as English:
     фри кар = three cars. Plural marking on the noun is still required even with an
     explicit count (no "singular after numbers" rule, unlike some real languages).
CN2. Ordinal + noun compounds (секонд трай = second try) follow the same word-order rule
     as CN1: ordinal precedes the noun, never follows it.
CN3. Fractions combine with a following noun without a linking particle: хаф пицца = half
     a pizza, ту фёрдс кейк = two-thirds of a cake — "of" is never expressed separately.
CN4. Negative numbers (не- prefix per the numeric system) may only prefix the numeral
     itself, never a noun or verb; не-ван кар is invalid, ит из не-ван = it is negative one
     is valid as a standalone numeric statement.
CN5. Large compound numbers built from hundred/thousand/million chain left-to-right with
     no internal connector, matching English reading order: ту миллион фаузанд ту
     хандред = two million one thousand two hundred (leading "one" before thousand/hundred
     may be dropped, matching casual English "two million, thousand two hundred").
CN6. Clock-time expressions (oclock, half past, quarter to) are treated as fixed multi-word
     lexical units for word-order purposes — they do not decompose under CN1's numeral+noun
     rule even though they contain numeral-like elements.
CN7. Quantity words (сам, мени, фью, ол, etc.) occupy the same pre-noun slot as explicit
     numerals and are mutually exclusive with them in one noun phrase — мени кар и фри кар
     is invalid; use either the quantity word or the exact number, not both.
CN8. Doubling/tripling (дабл, трипл) act as verbs or pre-noun intensifiers depending on
     context: дабл ит = double it (verb use), дабл потрен = double portion (pre-noun use);
     the form itself does not change between the two uses.
CN9. A percentage combines a number directly with перцент, no article or connector
     needed: фифти перцент = fifty percent, ту хандред перцент = two hundred percent.
CN10. Multiplication in casual speech (as opposed to the formal таймз operator) may use
      the pre-noun intensifiers дабл/трипл for x2/x3 only; x4 and beyond must use the
      formal numeral + таймз construction — фор таймз, not a coined quadruple-word.
CN11. Ranges ("three to five") place ту between the two numbers with no additional
      marking: фри ту файв = three to five. This ту is the directional/goal particle
      from Section D, reused here rather than a separate range-specific word.
CN12. When a numeral modifies a nightmare-tier coinage (Section: Nightmare Words) that
      is inherently uncountable in meaning (e.g. a mood word like клорн), the numeral is
      read as counting instances/episodes of that state, not discrete physical objects.
SECTION L — GENDERED PHRASING & SPEECH-STYLE RULES (GP1–GP16)
These rules govern how a whole utterance — not just a single word's marker — shifts
depending on the gender of the person being spoken about or spoken to, and how that
differs between writing and speech. They build on Section A (GA1–GA14) but apply at the
sentence/phrasing level rather than the single-word level.
GP1. When the subject of a sentence is fem-marked, any adjective describing that subject
     agrees by taking ф- as well, even if the adjective is several words away from the
     noun: фше из фстронг энд фсмарт — not фше из стронг энд смарт.
GP2. When speaking directly TO someone (second person), gender marking on йау itself is
     never used — йау stays invariant regardless of the addressee's gender; only third-
     person descriptions and self-reference (per GA12) carry optional gender marking.
GP3. Written registers (notes, documents, Standard-mode text) mark gender explicitly at
     first mention of a referent and may drop it on repeated mentions in the same
     paragraph; spoken/Casual registers mark gender on every mention for clarity, since
     listeners can't glance back at an earlier sentence.
GP4. A question asked ABOUT a specific person's action uses that person's gender marker
     on the verb's descriptive complement if one exists, but never on the question
     particle ли itself, which stays invariant: хе гуд ли? not хе фгуд ли? (invalid).
GP5. When retelling a story about a fem-marked person in Hard/Nightmare mode, the ф-
     ligature (per GA10) may be dropped after its first appearance in the retelling and
     recovered from context, but only if no other referent could be confused for it.
GP6. Compliments and insults directed at a person take that person's gender marker on
     the descriptive word itself, never on the exclamation or particle framing it: же,
     фсмарт ше! (seriously, she's smart!) — же stays unmarked per GA6.
GP7. When a sentence describes an action done TO a gendered object pronoun (him/her),
     the gender marking lives on the object pronoun itself (хим vs. хэр) and is never
     additionally repeated on the verb or on any adjective describing the action.
GP8. Formal/written apologies, congratulations, and condolences addressed to a specific
     person mark that person's gender on the noun of address if one is used (e.g. "friend,"
     "colleague") but not on фиксed formulaic phrases (плиз, сорри, конгрэтс), which are
     invariant regardless of who they're directed at.
GP9. In a sentence with a fem-marked subject and a masc-marked object in the same clause,
     word order alone (SVO) disambiguates who is who — gender marking is a texture layer
     on top of syntax, never a substitute for correct word order (ties to GA6).
GP10. When two speakers of different genders are quoted in the same passage (per DC4's
      reported-speech rule), each quote carries its speaker's own gender marking
      independently; the marking never bleeds from one quoted speaker into the other's line.
GP11. A generic/hypothetical person ("someone," "anyone," per the indefinite pronoun
      table) defaults to unmarked per GA2 and stays unmarked throughout the sentence even
      if later context reveals a specific gender — switch to a specific pronoun instead
      of retroactively marking the indefinite one.
GP12. Nicknames and terms of endearment may carry their own fixed gender marking that
      does NOT have to agree with the referent's marking elsewhere in the sentence, since
      endearment terms are treated as frozen vocabulary items (similar to WR12's
      contraction exemption) rather than productively-marked descriptions.
GP13. When writing dialogue in Standard mode for a worldbuilding/creative document (per
      RD8), gender marking on a character's speech tags (сэй, эск, реплай) is optional
      speech-tag verb itself, which stays invariant.
GP14. A sentence expressing group praise or blame where the group is gender-marked as a
      whole (per GA13) does not also require marking each individual action-word inside
      that sentence — the group marker covers the whole clause's gendered reading once.
GP15. Politeness downgrading/upgrading (per RD12) and gender marking are fully
      independent axes — softening or formalizing a sentence's register never adds or
      removes gender marking that was already present on its own terms.
GP16. When gender is genuinely unknown at the time of speaking but becomes known mid-
      conversation, the speaker may switch from н- to ф-/unmarked starting from the next
      new sentence; going back to correct already-spoken sentences is not required or
      expected — DXN1 doesn't retroactively re-mark completed utterances.

GENDER MARKING QUICK REFERENCE (ties to Section GA rules):
Default/masc (zero marker): хе, хис, химсэлф.
Feminine (ф- prefix): фше, фхэр, фхэрсэлф — ф- only attaches to she/her-line forms,
it does not attach to хе (he) since GA2 defines masculine as the zero-marked default.
Neutral (н- prefix): нит, нзей, нземсэлф — used when gender is unknown or the referent
is the singular-they/neutral pronoun set above.
Per GA2, masculine is always the zero-marked default; per GA4, neutral н- is never a
substitute for feminine ф- when the referent's gender is actually known to be female.

EMPIRE FOODS — DXN1 ORIGINAL DISHES (v5.7)
These are invented dishes native to the DXN1 world/empire — not translations of real
food, but original culture-words with their own flavor identity and lore hooks.
вречкейк - "wreck-cake" — a dense, heavily-layered dessert reserved for DXN1-STUDIOS
launch events; the name references its structural weight rather than any incident.
глоусуп - "glow-soup" — a broth dish with a faint bioluminescent tint, associated with
the ghost-/glitch-themed districts.
турборап - "turbo-wrap" — a compact handheld wrap built for speed, the empire's
equivalent of a burrito; common in gamer-culture districts.
мегамит - "mega-meat" — a large grilled skewer dish served at formal celebrations,
named with the мега- prefix from the word-building kit.
кривброд - "twisted-bread" — a braided, pretzel-adjacent bread named with the крив-
(broken/twisted) prefix, sold by vendors in the Hard-mode-coded districts.
дарксвит - "dark-sweet" — a bitter, dark chocolate-adjacent confection using the дарк-
prefix, tied culturally to late-night coding sessions.
неофрут - "neo-fruit" — a glowing fruit using the нео- prefix, cultivated exclusively
in the empire's greenhouse-zones; sweet with a sour aftertaste.
хардстью - "hard-stew" — a thick, slow-cooked stew using the hard- prefix; standard
sustenance after a long build/grind session.
протокейк - "proto-cake" — an early, experimental version of вречкейк; bakers use the
прото- prefix to mark unfinalized recipe drafts.

NUMERIC SYSTEM (v5.8)
DXN1 numbers stay close to their English roots so they're guessable at a glance, with
Cyrillic spelling and Hard-mode vowel compression following the same rules as every
other word class in the system.
Core digits (0-10):
Teens (11-19) — built on the ten root + digit, matching English teen-stacking:
Tens (20-90):
Compounding rule: tens + digit stack directly, no connector — твенти-ван = 21,
фёрти-фор = 44, найнти-найн = 99. Hard mode drops the hyphen entirely: твнтвн.
Large values:
Structure follows English: ту хандред = 200, фаузанд ту хандред фёрти-фор = 1,244.
No separate word is needed for "and" — DXN1 numbers chain directly like English does.
Ordinals (root + -ф or -рд, matching the English pattern rather than reinventing one):
Math operators:
plus - плас | Meaning: плюс | Casual: плас | Hard: плс | Type: operator

equals - иквалз | Meaning: равно | Casual: иквалз | Hard: иквл | Type: operator
Example: ту плас ту иквалз фор = two plus two equals four.

Fractions build as ordinal-root + noun, matching English: ван квортер = one quarter,

не-ван = negative one, не-фифтин = negative fifteen. Hard mode compresses to нван, нффтн.

SECTION M — GRAMMAR COMPLETION RULES (GC1–GC14)
These fill the remaining structural gaps: relative clauses, comparison, passive voice,
and a wider conjunction set.
Relative clauses:
GC1. A relative clause attaches with ху (for people) or зат (for things/animals),
     placed directly after the noun it describes: зе мэн ху ранс = the man who runs.
     зе кар зат брок = the car that broke.
GC2. When the relativized element is the object, not the subject, ху/зат still comes
     right after the noun, and the clause keeps normal SVO order with a gap where the
     object would be: зе бук зат и рид = the book that I read.
GC3. Relative clauses referring to a place use вер instead of зат: зе хаус вер и лив =
     the house where I live.
Comparatives & superlatives:
GC4. Comparative degree is marked with мор before the adjective for multi-syllable
     roots, or suffix -эр directly on short roots: мор бьютифул = more beautiful,
     but биггэр = bigger, фастэр = faster.
GC5. "Than" in a comparison is зэн, placed after the compared item: хи из фастэр зэн ми
     = he is faster than me.
GC6. Superlative degree uses зе мост before multi-syllable adjectives, or suffix -эст
     on short roots: зе мост бьютифул = the most beautiful, биггэст = biggest.
GC7. Equal comparison ("as X as") uses эз...эз bracketing the adjective: хи из эз
     толл эз хёр = he is as tall as her.
Passive voice:
GC8. Passive voice is formed with би + past participle (-ед/-эн form of the verb),
     with the agent optionally marked by бай: зе кар вос фикст (бай хим) = the car was
     fixed (by him).
GC9. Passive voice keeps normal tense marking on би itself (был би, буд би), never on
     the participle: ит был би брокен = it was broken (past passive).
GC10. Passive is avoided in Casual mode in favor of an unmarked-subject active
     construction ("зей фикст ит" = they fixed it) except when the agent is genuinely
     unknown or irrelevant — this matches GC8's optional-agent design.
Expanded conjunctions:
GC11. соу marks result/consequence: ит рейнд, соу и стейд ин = it rained, so I stayed in.
GC12. бикоз marks cause, placed at the head of the causal clause, which may come before
      or after the main clause: и стейд ин бикоз ит рейнд, or бикоз ит рейнд, и стейд ин.
GC13. олзоу marks concession ("although"): олзоу ит рейнд, и вент аут = although it
      rained, I went out. Distinct from бат, which joins two contrasting main clauses.
GC14. анлес marks a negative condition ("unless"): и вонт гоу анлес ю кам = I won't go
      unless you come. Functions like иф + не combined into one fixed connector.

NATIVE COINAGES — NON-TRANSLITERATED CORE WORDS (v6.0)
Up to now, almost every DXN1 word is a phonetic respelling of its English root. This
section breaks that pattern on purpose: these are original coined roots for the most
fundamental everyday concepts, built from scratch rather than borrowed sound-for-sound
from English. This is what gives the language actual identity instead of just being
"English in Cyrillic." These roots are irregular by design — they don't have to sound
like their English meaning at all, and that's the point.
Core greetings & social words:
хейлор - hello (casual, most common greeting; хейлор бро is a fixed combo)
скева - goodbye / see you (short, clipped — used constantly, replaces the English-root бай)
да-крон - yes (emphatic, "yes for real" — distinct from casual да borrowed elsewhere)
нольва - no (flat refusal, harder-edged than a simple English-root "ноу")
плисат - please (softer than the transliterated плиз; used in genuine requests)
данкор - thank you (the default "thanks," used constantly in daily speech)
сорим - sorry (a real apology, heavier than a casual "ой")
дружка - friend (warm, close-friend register — not the neutral "френд")
вражин - enemy / rival (someone actively against you, not just "someone you dislike")
Core life/world concepts:
дом-крин - home (not just "house" — the felt sense of home, belonging)
жизнир - life (the abstract concept, distinct from "alive" as a state)
смерка - death (blunt, matter-of-fact — no softening built into the root)
душир - soul / inner self
разум-ко - mind / mental clarity
сердцав - heart (emotional center, not the organ — the organ stays харт, transliterated)
покольд - silence (heavy, deliberate silence — not just "no sound")
хаосвин - chaos (the felt experience of chaos, not just disorder)
стройка - order / structure (the calm opposite of хаосвин)
крепса - strength / power (personal strength, not physical size)
слабко - weakness / fragility
однавел - alone / solitude (the state, can be neutral or heavy depending on tone)
вместар - together / unity
навсегрин - forever
никогдир - never
надёжка - hope
страхол - fear (deep, instinctive fear — not just "scared")
любовир - love (deep, not romantic-specific — romantic love uses a separate word below)
ненавидж - hate
Romantic/relationship-specific (distinct from любовир above):
сердцелюб - romantic love specifically (the "in love" feeling)
разлюбка - falling out of love / the fading of a relationship
тоскамой - longing for someone specific, missing them deeply
Weather/nature (native, distinct from transliterated versions elsewhere):
небеско - sky (poetic register, distinct from the plain transliterated скай)
землика - earth/ground (grounded, physical sense)
огнёр - fire (elemental, not just "flame")
водарь - water (elemental register)
ночевин - night (the felt atmosphere of night, distinct from just "nighttime")
рассветко - dawn / first light
Usage note: these native roots follow all the same productive-suffix rules from Section B
(WR1–WR16) — e.g. хейлор can still take -инг or -ер forms if a learner wants to build on
it — but they are never replaced or "fixed" by a transliterated equivalent. Where a
native root exists, it is the preferred word in Standard and Casual mode; the older
transliterated form (e.g. хай, бай, лав) still exists but reads as more casual/lazy by
comparison, the way slang sometimes displaces a "proper" word in a real language.
More original roots, same rules as Wave 1: built from scratch, not sound-derived from
English, preferred over the transliterated equivalent in Standard/Casual speech.
Time concepts:
седмица - week (native, distinct from the transliterated "уик")
зорька - morning (specifically the early-morning feel, not just "AM")
сумерка - evening / dusk
полноч - midnight (literal "full-night" feel, heavier than the transliterated мидnight)
скорень - soon (a felt "coming very shortly," stronger than the plain "сун")
давнеч - long ago / a long time back
нынеко - right now, this exact moment (more emphatic than plain "нау")
всегдар - always (native root, replaces relying only on "олвейз")
Common actions:
глядеть - to look/gaze (a longer, more deliberate look than the plain "лук")
творить - to make/create (creative-sense making, distinct from the plain "мейк")
ломать - to break (deliberate breaking, distinct from an accidental "брейк")
беречь - to protect/take care of (protective sense, stronger than plain "протект")
терпеть - to endure/put up with (distinct from plain "endure," carries weight)
искать - to search/seek (deliberate searching, distinct from casual "лук фор")
делить - to share/divide (distinct from the casual transliterated "шэр")
верить - to believe/trust (deep trust, distinct from the plain "билив")
Qualities & states:
крепкий - solid/reliable (a person or thing you can count on)
хрупкий - fragile (physically or emotionally delicate)
пустой - empty/hollow (can describe a room or a feeling)
живой - alive/vivid (full of life, more than the plain "алайв")
тихий - quiet/calm (a gentle quiet, distinct from покольд's heavier silence)
ясный - clear (mentally clear or a clear sky — dual use)
тёмный - dark (physically or emotionally, native root)
светлый - bright/light-filled (opposite of тёмный)
Food & eating (native, for the most basic verbs only — specific foods stay transliterated):
кушать - to eat (everyday native verb, more natural than the transliterated "ит")
пить - to drink (native, replaces "дринк" in natural speech)
готовить - to cook (native, the actual act of cooking — dishes themselves stay transliterated)
голодный - hungry (native, stronger felt sense than "хангри")
сытый - full/satisfied after eating
Work & effort:
трудиться - to work hard/labor (heavier than the plain transliterated "ворк")
стараться - to try one's best (deeper effort than the plain "трай")
уставать - to get tired/worn out (native, distinct from plain "тайрд")
отдыхать - to rest/relax (native, the actual act of resting)
спать - to sleep (native, replaces the transliterated "слип" in natural speech)
Movement:
идти - to walk/go (native, everyday movement verb)
бежать - to run (native, replaces "ран" in natural speech)
лететь - to fly (native — also used figuratively for moving fast)
ехать - to travel/ride (by vehicle specifically, distinct from идти on foot)
Usage note: as with Wave 1, these coexist with their transliterated counterparts, but
carry more emotional or literary weight — a DXN1 speaker reaching for искать instead of
"лук фор," or творить instead of "мейк," is choosing the heavier, more native-feeling
word on purpose. This is the layer that separates casual filler speech from writing
meant to actually land (song lyrics, the book, worldbuilding prose).
500 more, hand-built across 25 categories, transliterated phonetic-Cyrillic convention.
