[MASTER SYSTEM ADDENDUM v7.0 — GOVERNING PRINCIPLES]
MS01. DXN1 meaning is primary; visual style is secondary whenever the two conflict.
MS02. Every standard form must have a recoverable English interpretation.
MS03. A sentence may be judged grammatical even when its spelling is highly compressed.
MS04. New grammar should be built from existing particles before inventing a new particle.
MS05. New particles should have one dominant job and no more than two closely related jobs.
MS06. A root should keep one semantic center across casual, standard, and hard forms.
MS07. Hard mode may remove letters, but it must preserve enough landmarks to recover the root.
MS08. Nightmare mode may sacrifice immediate readability for recognizable structure.
MS09. Script mixing is a feature and does not automatically count as an error.
MS10. Latin is preferred for exact names, URLs, code, file paths, commands, and technical identifiers.
MS11. Cyrillic is preferred for ordinary lexical content even when a Latin spelling would be shorter.
MS12. Repeated letters may encode emotion, duration, hesitation, sarcasm, or intensity.
MS13. Capitalization may encode emphasis, shouting, labels, or mode boundaries.
MS14. Punctuation may carry grammatical meaning in chat mode.
MS15. Dictionary entries should identify the English headword, DXN1 standard form, and optional casual/hard forms.
MS16. When two forms compete, the form with clearer semantic recovery wins in standard mode.
MS17. Slang may violate textbook spelling while remaining valid DXN1.
MS18. Back-translation should recover intent rather than mechanically reproduce every surface feature.
MS19. Culture words may remain untranslated when translation would destroy the DXN1 identity.
MS20. Every productive affix should have a stable semantic direction.
MS21. Every grammar extension should be compatible with the default subject-plus-predicate architecture.
MS22. Ambiguity is acceptable in casual speech but should be actively reduced in standard writing.
MS23. The same token may act as root, compound element, or slang particle when context permits.
MS24. DXN1 does not require Russian phonology merely because Cyrillic is used.
MS25. English-first syntax remains the baseline unless a documented DXN1 rule overrides it.
MS26. System rules are prioritized in the order: meaning, grammar, readability, style, compression.
MS27. Local slang conventions may override default spelling only inside their declared register.
MS28. A sentence can contain ordinary English words without ceasing to be DXN1 if its grammar remains DXN1-like.
MS29. Machine-readable notes, URLs, code, usernames, and commands are always allowed to remain Latin.
MS30. When a new rule conflicts with an older rule, the newer explicit rule governs while the old rule remains valid historically.
[CORE WORD ORDER & CLAUSE RULES]
SX01. Default order is SUBJECT + TENSE/ASPECT + VERB + OBJECT + PLACE + TIME + MOOD.
SX02. Adverbs normally sit immediately before the element they modify.
SX03. Frequency adverbs prefer the position before the main verb.
SX04. Place phrases normally follow the object unless place is topicalized.
SX05. Time phrases may move to the front when the speaker wants a time frame emphasized.
SX06. Topic-first order is allowed with то marking the fronted topic.
SX07. Contrastive objects may be fronted and followed by то.
SX08. Questions may preserve statement order and add ли.
SX09. Wh-questions place the question word in the semantic slot being questioned.
SX10. Commands normally omit the subject when the addressee is obvious.
SX11. Vocatives are separated by punctuation or a pause.
SX12. Negative clauses place не before the main lexical verb.
SX13. Negative modal constructions place не before the modal marker when the whole proposition is denied.
SX14. An auxiliary tense marker never replaces the lexical verb unless the context already supplies the lexical verb.
SX15. Two finite lexical verbs may occur in sequence only when the second behaves as a complement.
SX16. Coordination uses explicit connectors when omission could cause ambiguity.
SX17. Subordinate clauses may be introduced by иф, вен, виле, бекаусе, or other clause-linking particles.
SX18. Relative clauses may follow the noun they describe.
SX19. Short conversational fragments are valid if the missing material is obvious.
SX20. Echo questions may repeat only the questioned element.
SX21. Tag-like confirmation may use ли or же.
SX22. Topic chains may omit repeated subjects across adjacent clauses.
SX23. Anaphoric pronouns should be preferred when repeating a noun would feel heavy.
SX24. Parallel clauses should use parallel marker placement whenever practical.
SX25. Standard mode prefers predictable constituent order over dramatic inversion.
SX26. Hard mode permits one major inversion per sentence before readability falls.
SX27. Nightmare mode may chain fragments, but each fragment should still expose its semantic head.
SX28. Sentence-final mood markers attach to the whole clause rather than only the final noun.
SX29. Parenthetical comments should be visually separated with commas, dashes, or brackets.
SX30. Quoted material keeps its original internal word order unless it is intentionally translated into DXN1.
[NOUN, DETERMINER & QUANTITY RULES]
NO01. Singular nouns use the base lexical form.
NO02. Plural nouns may use -s in general standard usage.
NO03. Plural -z is favored after voiced or sharp slang endings when it improves rhythm.
NO04. Plural -и and -ы may be used as stylized alternatives in casual or hard mode.
NO05. Explicit numerals normally precede the noun.
NO06. An indefinite singular noun may use а or ан when an article-like distinction is useful.
NO07. The definite marker зе may precede an identifiable noun phrase.
NO08. Repeated nouns can be reduced after the first mention in casual mode.
NO09. Mass nouns normally remain unmarked unless a unit is being counted.
NO10. Containers and units may be used to count otherwise mass-like nouns.
NO11. Collective meaning may be encoded with -ерс or a group-root compound.
NO12. Quantifiers such as море and лесс precede the noun they quantify.
NO13. Very large quantity may be intensified with mega-, ультра-, or -макс.
NO14. Very small quantity may be marked with micro- or мини-style builders.
NO15. A noun used as a modifier normally stays unchanged.
NO16. Compound nouns should place the semantic head last unless a common slang compound fixes another order.
NO17. Possessive marking may use a possessive pronoun before the noun.
NO18. Possessive suffixes are optional and should not be stacked with identical possessive marking.
NO19. Names normally keep their original spelling unless a DXN1 stylization is culturally established.
NO20. Titles may precede a name without article marking.
NO21. Occupational nouns may be created with -ер when the meaning is transparent.
NO22. Action-result nouns may use -ед when a completed artifact or state is intended.
NO23. Process nouns may use -инг for an ongoing activity or vibe.
NO24. Places and domains may use -зона when an area or scene is intended.
NO25. Abstract noun formation should favor existing roots plus productive suffixes.
NO26. If a noun has several dictionary senses, context should determine the sense before a new spelling is invented.
NO27. Plural markers may be omitted after numerals in extremely compressed hard mode if the quantity is unmistakable.
NO28. Standard writing should avoid mixing two plural strategies in the same noun phrase.
NO29. Collective groups may remain formally singular when the verb treats the group as one unit.
NO30. Individual members of a collective use ordinary plural marking when the focus shifts from group to members.
NO31. Zero article is allowed for generic plural or abstract statements.
[ADJECTIVE, ADVERB & COMPARISON RULES]
AD01. Basic adjectives may precede the noun they modify.
AD02. Predicative adjectives follow a copular or implied be structure.
AD03. Adjectives do not require Russian-style case agreement.
AD04. Adjectives normally do not change for number.
AD05. Adjectives may be intensified with very, hyper-, mega-, turbo-, or repeated letters.
AD06. Adverbial use may be inferred from position when the meaning remains clear.
AD07. An explicit adverbial form may use a dedicated suffix such as -ly when needed for disambiguation.
AD08. Comparative meaning uses more before the adjective.
AD09. Superlative meaning may use most before the adjective or -макс in slang.
AD10. Less uses лесс before the adjective.
AD11. Equality uses as + adjective + as when an explicit comparison is needed.
AD12. Contrastive comparison may use more X than Y in English-like structure.
AD13. Absolute intensification may use ultra- or peak- without requiring a comparison set.
AD14. Negated comparison places не before the comparison predicate.
AD15. Color terms may act as ordinary adjectives without agreement endings.
AD16. Compound adjectives may join two roots with a hyphen or no-space compound.
AD17. Repeated adjective forms may indicate playful or exaggerated intensity.
AD18. Adjectives can be nominalized when the noun meaning is obvious from context.
AD19. An adjective used as a category label should normally keep its base spelling.
AD20. Hard mode may compress repeated adjective endings if the root remains visible.
AD21. Casual mode permits slang adjective compounds freely.
AD22. Standard mode prefers one clear adjective head per noun phrase.
AD23. When multiple adjectives occur, opinion/style adjectives normally come before concrete descriptive adjectives.
AD24. Numeric descriptors should usually precede qualitative descriptors.
AD25. Degree particles should stay next to the adjective they modify.
AD26. Nearly and almost expressions should not be confused with completed-state markers.
AD27. A descriptive root can become a person noun through -ер when semantically natural.
AD28. A descriptive root can become an abstract state with -ность-like conceptual suffixes only after the builder system explicitly licenses one.
AD29. Contradictory adjectives may be intentionally stacked for irony.
AD30. Context, not morphology alone, determines whether a word is literal or slang.
[PRONOUN, REFERENCE & ANAPHORA RULES]
PR01. Subject pronouns use the established core set unless omission is clearer.
PR02. Object pronouns may be used without changing the verb.
PR03. Possessive pronouns normally precede the owned noun.
PR04. Standalone possessives may appear after a copular structure.
PR05. Reflexive meaning uses the reflexive system already established by the language.
PR06. Pronoun omission is allowed when the subject is recoverable from context.
PR07. Pronoun repetition is allowed for emphasis or contrast.
PR08. Explicit pronouns become more useful when a clause changes subject.
PR09. Names may replace pronouns when multiple referents could be confused.
PR10. Demonstratives зис, зат, зесе, and зосе distinguish near/far and singular/plural reference.
PR11. Demonstratives may stand alone as pronouns.
PR12. Indefinite pronouns may be compounds built from common roots such as some-, any-, every-, or no-.
PR13. Nobody and nothing compounds should preserve the no- semantic family.
PR14. Someone and something compounds should preserve the some- semantic family.
PR15. Question pronouns occupy the slot corresponding to the requested information.
PR16. Who refers primarily to people; what refers primarily to things or concepts.
PR17. Which may select from an explicit or implied set.
PR18. That can introduce a complement clause when the context could otherwise be ambiguous.
PR19. Pronoun reference should favor the closest grammatically compatible antecedent.
PR20. A discourse topic may maintain reference across several clauses without repeating a pronoun.
PR21. Singular they-style reference may use the established they form when gender is unknown or intentionally unspecified.
PR22. Gender markers should not be added merely because a pronoun already indicates gender.
PR23. Possessive chains should be kept short in standard writing.
PR24. Reflexive forms are preferred when actor and affected participant are the same.
PR25. Emphatic self-reference may repeat a pronoun plus a reflexive marker.
PR26. Pronouns can be used as standalone replies.
PR27. Elliptical replies such as yes, no, maybe, and okay are grammatically valid conversation turns.
PR28. Hard mode may compress common pronouns further when the result stays unique.
PR29. Nightmare mode may encode pronouns with context tags, but this is optional and not standard.
PR30. Pronoun choice should preserve social tone and avoid accidental hostility.
[TENSE, ASPECT & TIMELINE RULES]
TA01. был marks a completed or past-oriented event.
TA02. буд marks future orientation.
TA03. из marks an ongoing or progressive event.
TA04. ду marks a completed/perfect result.
TA05. не negates the proposition.
TA06. ли marks a question when interrogative word order is not enough.
TA07. Markers normally appear before the lexical verb.
TA08. Multiple aspect markers may stack when each adds distinct information.
TA09. буд + из expresses future ongoing action.
TA10. был + из expresses past ongoing action.
TA11. был + ду expresses a past completed result when the result remains relevant.
TA12. буд + ду may express a future completed state.
TA13. Repeated tense markers are avoided unless the first is a discourse echo or contrast.
TA14. Time adverbs may reinforce but do not automatically replace tense markers.
TA15. today, tomorrow, yesterday, soon, and later may clarify a marker's intended timeline.
TA16. An already-completed event may use ду plus an appropriate time phrase.
TA17. A habitual action may use a present-like unmarked verb with a frequency adverb.
TA18. Future intention may use буд even when the action is scheduled or planned.
TA19. Past experience may use ду when the exact time is not central.
TA20. Continuous emotion or state may use из when the speaker wants temporary duration emphasized.
TA21. Stative verbs may omit iz when the state is understood as general rather than temporary.
TA22. Time clauses should use a clear connector such as вен or виле.
TA23. Since/until meanings should be expressed with explicit time relations rather than overloaded tense markers.
TA24. Sequence-of-events writing should normally keep chronological tense consistent.
TA25. Sudden narrative shifts may deliberately switch tense for dramatic effect.
TA26. Casual speech may drop markers when adverbs make the timeline obvious.
TA27. Standard explanatory prose should keep markers when a tense contrast matters.
TA28. Hard mode may use one marker for a chain of clauses when all share the same timeline.
TA29. Nightmare mode may rely heavily on discourse context, but it must preserve at least one recoverable timeline cue per major event.
TA30. Chronological clarity outranks stylistic compression.
[NEGATION, QUESTIONS & POLARITY]
NQ01. не is the default clause negator.
NQ02. Negation normally occurs before the main lexical predicate.
NQ03. Double negation is allowed only when it has an intentional semantic effect.
NQ04. не should not be repeated merely for emphasis.
NQ05. Question particle ли can be clause-final or placed near the questioned predicate in casual style.
NQ06. Wh-questions do not require ли when the question word already makes interrogative force clear.
NQ07. Yes/no questions may be formed with ли without changing word order.
NQ08. Alternative questions use ор between the alternatives.

NQ10. Negative questions may distinguish surprise from simple request for confirmation.
NQ11. Rhetorical questions may omit the normal answer expectation.
NQ12. Imperative negatives use не plus the command predicate.
NQ13. Question words may be left uninflected.
NQ14. Who, what, where, when, why, and how should each occupy the semantic slot they query.
NQ15. Why-questions should normally use a causal connector in the answer when relevant.
NQ16. How-questions may ask manner, degree, means, or process; context decides.
NQ17. Where-questions distinguish location from movement when possible.
NQ18. When-questions distinguish event time from duration when necessary.
NQ19. Question punctuation normally uses ? in standard writing.
NQ20. Casual chat may use multiple question marks for emotional intensity.
NQ21. Hard mode may omit the question mark when ли already carries the signal.
NQ22. Nightmare mode may use symbols or fragments, but the question target must remain recoverable.
NQ23. Negative imperatives should remain concise.
NQ24. Partial agreement can be expressed with yes/no plus a correction clause.
NQ25. A direct answer may repeat only the questioned predicate for brevity.
NQ26. Surprise may be marked with же in a question.
NQ27. Uncertainty may pair a question form with ну or мэйбе.
NQ28. Answering a wh-question with a single slot-filler is fully grammatical.
NQ29. Clarification questions may repeat the ambiguous word with rising intonation.
NQ30. Question chains should avoid stacking multiple ли markers unless each belongs to a separate clause.

[VOICE, VALENCY & VERB-FAMILY RULES]

PT22. URLs are copied exactly.
PT23. Email addresses are copied exactly.
PT24. File paths are copied exactly.
PT25. Code blocks are not subject to ordinary orthographic transformation unless specifically requested.
PT26. Markdown headings can remain in Latin or be stylized.
PT27. Lists may use bullets or numbering without changing sentence grammar.
PT28. Newlines may create discourse boundaries in chat mode.
PT29. Line breaks may replace commas in poetic or dramatic text.
PT30. Standard prose should not rely on line breaks alone for essential grammar.
PT31. Nightmare formatting may use symbols as visual separators.
[ERROR HANDLING, AMBIGUITY & SELF-CORRECTION]
ER01. When a token is unknown, infer from English-like root shape and context before declaring it invalid.
ER02. If a sentence has one obvious typo, preserve the intended root during interpretation.
ER03. Unknown suffixes should be treated as possible productive builders before being rejected.
ER04. Unknown prefixes should be treated as possible semantic modifiers.
ER05. Mixed-script tokens should not be split unless there is evidence for a compound.
ER06. Ambiguous word boundaries may be resolved by semantic plausibility.
ER07. Repeated letters should be ignored for lexical lookup after emotional intent is recognized.
ER08. Hard-mode vowel deletion should not cause a new word to be invented accidentally.
ER09. If two parses are possible, prefer the one with simpler DXN1 grammar.
ER10. If two parses remain possible, prefer the reading supported by immediate context.
ER11. If context still cannot decide, preserve both interpretations.
ER12. Formal dictionaries should record common ambiguous forms with notes.
ER13. Corrections should prefer the canonical standard form.
ER14. Casual corrections may propose a shorter variant.
ER15. Self-correction can be written as wrong → corrected.
ER16. Meaning-preserving spelling variants may coexist.
ER17. Historical or community variants should not be deleted merely because a newer form is preferred.
ER18. An outdated form may be marked legacy rather than invalid.
ER19. A new word should not be introduced solely to fix a trivial typo.
ER20. Repeated accidental spellings may become slang if the community intentionally adopts them.
ER21. Grammar errors in a creative character voice may be deliberate.
ER22. An intentionally broken form should be marked as character/dialect style in formal documentation.
ER23. Dictionary editors should record whether a form is standard, casual, hard, nightmare, slang, dialectal, or legacy.
ER24. Examples should demonstrate the intended interpretation, not only the dictionary form.
ER25. Back-translation should report uncertainty when a source sentence was ambiguous.
ER26. Do not silently reinterpret a sentence into Russian grammar just because it is written in Cyrillic.
ER27. Do not force every borrowed word into an artificial native-looking root.
ER28. Keep the English semantic anchor visible when introducing unfamiliar vocabulary.
ER29. An error rule should never override a clearly documented creative convention.
ER30. Interpretation is allowed to be tolerant; generation should be systematic.
[DIALECT & COMMUNITY EXTENSION RULES]
DX01. A dialect can define its own pronunciation style without changing core meanings.
DX02. A dialect may introduce a small local particle set.
DX03. Dialect particles should be documented with examples.
DX04. A dialect may prefer one plural ending over another.
DX05. A dialect may prefer stronger or softer contractions.
DX06. Differences in spelling should be mapped back to one canonical root where possible.
DX07. Community slang can become canonical after sustained, recognizable use.
DX08. Canonicalization should not erase living slang variants.
DX09. New particles should be tested against existing particles for semantic overlap.
DX10. A dialect should not redefine a core pronoun accidentally.
DX11. Core tense markers should remain stable across major dialects unless the branch is explicitly marked divergent.
DX12. Dialect-specific vocabulary may coexist with the standard lexicon.
DX13. Local names should remain unchanged unless the community intentionally adopts a stylized form.
DX14. Regional humor may be encoded as vocabulary rather than grammar.
DX15. Pronunciation notes may be stored separately from spelling rules.
DX16. A dialect may favor more Latin script without becoming non-DXN1.
DX17. A dialect may favor more Cyrillic without changing its English-first identity.
DX18. Community spellings may be archived under version labels.
DX19. Version labels should not be used to imply that older speakers are wrong.
DX20. Dialect forms may be used as character voice markers in fiction.
DX21. Teaching materials should distinguish standard grammar from dialect flavor.
DX22. A new dialect rule should state its scope.
DX23. A dialect rule should state whether it is mandatory, preferred, or optional.
DX24. Dialect-specific shortcuts should not leak into standard documents without annotation.
DX25. Community innovations should be evaluated for recognizability.
DX26. Highly opaque innovations may remain subdialectal.
DX27. Any branch that changes sentence order should document how it maps to standard order.
DX28. Any branch that changes tense marking should document how it maps to the core markers.
DX29. Any branch can develop local idioms.
DX30. Idioms should be documented with literal and intended meanings.
[IDIOM, METAPHOR & FIGURATIVE MEANING RULES]
IM01. Idioms are allowed and may ignore literal compositional meaning.
IM02. An idiom should have a documented intended meaning if it becomes common.
IM03. Literal and figurative readings may coexist.
IM04. Context decides whether a phrase is literal or idiomatic.
IM05. Metaphorical compounds may use ordinary roots in novel combinations.
IM06. Gaming slang may become metaphorical outside gaming.
IM07. Tech vocabulary may be metaphorically applied to people, moods, or social situations.
IM08. Ghost-, glitch-, buff-, nerf-, lag-, and sync-style roots can extend metaphorically when the image is clear.
IM09. An idiom may preserve English word order even if the literal components would otherwise be built differently.
IM10. Creative writers may coin temporary idioms.
IM11. Temporary idioms should remain understandable from context.
IM12. Poetic compression may deliberately leave a metaphor underspecified.
IM13. Humor can depend on a literal/figurative double reading.
IM14. Repeated metaphor can create a cultural expression.
IM15. Culture words may have a narrower meaning inside the DXN1 community.
IM16. Lexicon notes should explain culture-specific senses.
IM17. Idioms should not be back-translated word-for-word when the intended meaning would be lost.
IM18. Teaching examples should label idiomatic uses when beginners could misread them.
IM19. Nightmare mode may compress an idiom into a single fused token.
IM20. Slang may lexicalize a metaphor after repeated use.
IM21. Metaphor does not require new grammar.
IM22. Figurative insults may be constructed from ordinary roots.
IM23. Positive praise may use gaming or aura vocabulary metaphorically.
IM24. Negative states may use cooked, lagged, crashed, or glitched metaphors when context supports them.
IM25. Movement metaphors can describe social or emotional changes.
IM26. Weather metaphors can describe mood.
IM27. Cold/hot may refer to literal temperature or social intensity.
IM28. Dark/bright may refer to lighting, mood, secrecy, or clarity.
IM29. Peak/max language may refer to performance or aesthetic quality.
IM30. Soft/hard may refer to tone, difficulty, or style.
[LEXICON GROWTH RULES — SAFE EXPANSION]
LX01. Prefer an existing core root before creating a new root.
LX02. Add a new root when no existing root expresses the needed semantic center cleanly.
LX03. Do not create near-duplicate roots for the same common meaning unless register differences justify them.
LX04. Maintain one canonical English headword per standard entry.
LX05. Store synonyms as linked entries rather than competing definitions.
LX06. Record whether a synonym is neutral, slang, technical, dialectal, or poetic.
LX07. Technical vocabulary can preserve specialized spellings.
LX08. Common words should favor easy Cyrillic recognition.
LX09. New slang should be short enough to survive chat usage.
LX10. New hard forms should preserve at least two strong root landmarks whenever practical.
LX11. Culture words may be coined from familiar DXN1 roots.
LX12. Abstract nouns should prefer transparent derivation.
LX13. People nouns should prefer agentive builders.
LX14. Location nouns should prefer -зона or another transparent place builder.
LX15. Process nouns should prefer -инг.
LX16. Completed-result nouns should prefer -ед.
LX17. Group nouns may prefer -ерс.
LX18. Maximum-style slang may prefer -макс.
LX19. A product or package concept may prefer -пак.
LX20. Repeated cyclic behavior may prefer -лооп.
LX21. Release/output behavior may prefer -дроп.
LX22. Continuous flow may prefer -стрим.
LX23. Synchronization may prefer -синк.
LX24. Craft/building may prefer -крафт.
LX25. Aura/visibility may prefer -глоу.
LX26. Style trends may prefer -вэйв.
LX27. Builder stacking should remain semantically compositional whenever possible.
LX28. An entry may be standard even if its source is slang when the community has normalized it.
LX29. Lexicon additions should include one example sentence.
LX30. Lexicon additions should avoid colliding with core particles.

[DXN1 / ДЖН1 NAMING & FINAL MICRO-RULES v7.1]
NAME RULE 01. OFFICIAL CYRILLIC NAME
- The canonical Cyrillic form of “DXN1” is ДЖН1.
- ДЖН1 is the preferred Cyrillic way to write the language name inside DXN1 text.
- The Latin form DXN1 remains valid for code, URLs, filenames, project names, technical labels,
  and situations where Latin script is required.
NAME RULE 02. WHY ДЖН1 EXISTS
- DXN1 is a Latin visual identifier, while ДЖН1 is its Cyrillic-native identity.
- The Cyrillic form is not a translation into Russian.
- ДЖН1 must be treated as one proper name, not as three separate lexical words.
- The numeral 1 is preserved exactly and is never replaced by a Cyrillic word in the standard form.
NAME RULE 03. CHARACTER MAPPING
- D -> Д
- X -> Ж
- N -> Н
- 1 -> 1
- Therefore: DXN1 -> ДЖН1.
- This mapping applies only to the official name unless another word specifically declares a mapping.
NAME RULE 04. SAYING “DXN1 LANGUAGE”
- Standard Cyrillic name: ДЖН1 лэнг.
- Casual form: ДЖН1 лэн.
- Hard form: ДЖН1лнг.
- Nightmare form: ДЖН1.
- “лэнг” is a language-name noun meaning “language / language system” in the DXN1 naming context.
- A speaker may also say “ДЖН1 язык” as a deliberately Russian-looking joke or alternate in-world form,
  but the default official expression is ДЖН1 лэнг.
NAME RULE 05. POSSESSIVE NAME FORMS
- “DXN1 language rules” -> ДЖН1 лэнг рулс.
- “DXN1 speaker” -> ДЖН1 спикэр.
- “in DXN1” -> ин ДЖН1.
- “written in DXN1” -> ритен ин ДЖН1.
- “learn DXN1” -> лирн ДЖН1.
- “I speak DXN1” -> и спик ДЖН1.
NAME RULE 06. LANGUAGE-AS-OBJECT
- When the language itself is the object of a verb, no article is required in the compact standard.
- Example: и лирн ДЖН1 = I learn DXN1.
- Example: и лике ДЖН1 = I like DXN1.
- “зе ДЖН1” is allowed when treating the language as a specific named system.
NAME RULE 07. PROPER-NAME CAPITALIZATION
- ДЖН1 is normally capitalized because it is a proper name.
- Derived forms may remain capitalized when they directly name the system:
  ДЖН1-лэнг, ДЖН1-спикэр, ДЖН1-мод, ДЖН1-кор.
- Generic derived slang may be lowercase after its meaning becomes independent:
  джн1зэр = a DXN1-style user/person (optional slang).
NAME RULE 08. HYPHEN RULE
- Hyphens are preferred when ДЖН1 directly modifies a named technical or cultural term:
  ДЖН1-лэнг, ДЖН1-док, ДЖН1-мод.
- A space is preferred when the following word behaves as a normal noun:
  ДЖН1 лэнг, ДЖН1 спикэр, ДЖН1 рулс.
- Never create confusing chains longer than three semantic parts in Standard mode.
NAME RULE 09. MIXED-SCRIPT PERMISSION
- DXN1 and ДЖН1 may coexist in one document.
- Use DXN1 when referring to the project/file/technical identifier.
- Use ДЖН1 when speaking naturally inside the language.
- Example: “DXN1 проект” is documentation style; “ДЖН1 лэнг” is native-style usage.
NAME RULE 10. NUMBER PRESERVATION
- Numeral 1 remains visually and grammatically stable.
- It may be pronounced as “ван” in speech-oriented writing, but the written official name stays ДЖН1.
- Do not pluralize the numeral itself.
NAME RULE 11. NEW LEXICAL RULES FOR SELF-REFERENCE
- лэнг = language/system.
- спикэр = speaker/user of a language.
- ридэр = reader of a language/text.
- рулс = rules.
- док = documentation/document.
- нейм = name.
- кор = core.
- мод = mode.
- верж = version.
RULE 12. SELF-REFERENCE SENTENCE
- ДЖН1 лэнг буд гроу = the DXN1 language will grow.
- и лирн ДЖН1 = I learn DXN1.
- зе рулс оф ДЖН1 = the rules of DXN1.
RULE 13. OFFICIAL SHORT NAME
- ДЖН1 alone is a complete valid reference to the language.
- Speakers do not need to repeat “лэнг” after it.
- “ДЖН1” may therefore mean the script, language, system, or cultural style when context makes the meaning clear.
RULE 14. CONTEXT PRIORITY
- If “ДЖН1” appears next to words like лэнг, рулс, спикэр, or док, interpret it as the language system.
- If it appears next to project/tech vocabulary, interpret it as the project or technical identifier.
- Context beats rigid translation.
RULE 15. VERSION TAGGING
- The language name may be versioned as ДЖН1 v7.1, ДЖН1 v8, etc.
- Do not change the proper-name mapping when the version changes.
RULE 16. MODE DISPLAY
- Casual: ДЖН1
- Standard: ДЖН1 лэнг
- Hard: ДЖН1лнг
- Nightmare: ДЖН1
- The shorter form is valid when the surrounding sentence already makes the meaning obvious.
RULE 17. SELF-CORRECTION
- If a writer uses “ДХН1” or another accidental rendering, Standard mode should normalize it to ДЖН1.
- Accidental Latin/cyrillic substitutions do not create a new dialect unless deliberately documented.
RULE 18. STYLE CONSISTENCY
- Do not alternate randomly between DXN1, ДЖН1, and unrelated spellings within a short sentence.
- Pick one based on script context and maintain it until the context changes.
RULE 19. NEW WORD FORMATION FOR CULTURE TERMS
- ДЖН1 + root can create named cultural concepts:
  ДЖН1-вэйв = DXN1 aesthetic/style wave.
  ДЖН1-кор = core DXN1 identity.
  ДЖН1-спик = speaking in DXN1.
  ДЖН1-крафт = creating new DXN1 words/rules.
RULE 20. FINAL IDENTITY RULE
- DXN1 is the Latin name.
- ДЖН1 is the Cyrillic name.
- Both refer to the same language.
- Neither form is Russian.
- The official Cyrillic spelling is ДЖН1 and should be treated as the default native written name.
END OF DXN1-LANGUAGE EXPANDED SYSTEM v7.1
GENDER SUFFIX SYSTEM — ДЖН1 v6.63.922
The official word-level gender system uses suffixes rather than prefixes when the
speaker wants to explicitly identify a person, role, title, or gendered reference.
FEMININE SUFFIX: -ью
MASCULINE SUFFIX: -ьж
GENDER RULE 1.
- -ью marks a word as female/feminine.
- -ьж marks a word as male/masculine.
- The unsuffixed form remains neutral/default unless context says otherwise.
GENDER RULE 2.
The gender suffix attaches directly to the end of the base word:
[root] + ью = feminine
[root] + ьж = masculine
GENDER RULE 3.
The suffix is used mainly for people and person-like roles, not ordinary objects.
GENDER RULE 4.
A gender suffix must not change the root's basic meaning. It only specifies gender.
GENDER RULE 5.
тичэp = teacher / teacher, unspecified
тичэpью = female teacher
тичэpьж = male teacher
френд = friend / unspecified friend
френдью = female friend
френдьж = male friend
лидэр = leader / unspecified leader
лидэрью = female leader
лидэрьж = male leader
критор = creator / unspecified creator
криторью = female creator
криторьж = male creator
студент = student / unspecified student
студентью = female student
студентьж = male student
GENDER RULE 6.
The suffix is added after normal derivation:
root + builder/suffix + gender suffix.
Example:
критор + -ер + ью = криторерью
GENDER RULE 7.
If a word already has a grammatical gender marker from an older/alternate system,
the new suffix system takes priority in v6.63.922. Do not use two competing gender
systems on the same word in Standard mode.
GENDER RULE 8.
Gender suffixes may be used with names, titles, occupations, relationship words,
and human descriptors when the distinction matters.
GENDER RULE 9.
Do not gender ordinary inanimate nouns merely because another language would assign
them grammatical gender. ДЖН1 gender is semantic: it normally refers to the person
being described.
GENDER RULE 10.
Pluralization comes after gender marking:
[root] + ью + plural
[root] + ьж + plural
френдьюс = female friends
френдьжс = male friends
GENDER RULE 11.
In Casual mode, gender suffixes may be shortened only if the meaning remains obvious.
In Standard mode, write the full -ью or -ьж.
GENDER RULE 12.
In Hard mode, the suffix may remain fully visible even when the root is compressed.
френдью -> фрндью
френдьж -> фрндьж
GENDER RULE 13.
In Nightmare mode, gender marking may be heavily compressed, but the final gender
identity must remain recoverable from context.
GENDER RULE 14.
Gender suffixes are never placed before the root.
Invalid: ьюфренд
Invalid: ьжфренд
Valid: френдью / френдьж
GENDER RULE 15.
The suffixes are pronounced as distinct endings and should not be confused with
ordinary root letters.
GENDER RULE 16.
A speaker can deliberately leave gender unspecified by using the bare root:
тичэp = teacher, gender not stated.
GENDER RULE 17.
If gender is already obvious from a proper name or sentence context, the suffix is
optional unless Standard writing specifically requires explicit gender marking.
GENDER RULE 18.
Pronouns can reinforce a gendered noun:
ше тичэрью = she is a female teacher.
хе тичэрьж = he is a male teacher.
GENDER RULE 19.
The suffix may also be used on relational nouns:
броью = female-coded sister-like/friend-bro reference when intentionally gendered.
матеью = female mate/friend.
матеьж = male mate/friend.
GENDER RULE 20.
The suffix system is productive. A newly coined human-role word can receive -ью or
-ьж without needing a separate dictionary entry, provided the base word is valid.

ДЖН1 DAILY WORDBOOK EXTENSION — v6.63.925
Purpose: a large everyday expansion of the ДЖН1 vocabulary. These entries are lexical roots;
productive endings below can turn many roots into people, actions, tools, places, adjectives,
and abstract ideas. The original book remains the authority for existing forms.
PRODUCTIVE ENDINGS — THE WORD-GROWTH SYSTEM
END-01: Bare root = the simplest noun/verb/adjective meaning of the English root.
END-02: -ер creates a person/agent who does the root action: рид → ридэр = reader.
END-03: -ью marks a female/feminine human role after the complete word: ридэрью = female reader.
END-04: -ьж marks a male/masculine human role after the complete word: ридэрьж = male reader.
END-05: -инг creates an activity, process, or ongoing vibe: плэй → плэйинг = playing/activity.
END-06: -ед creates a completed result/state when semantically natural: фикc → фиксeд = fixed/result state.
END-07: -ка creates a tool/object used for the root action: клин → клинка = cutting tool/object.
END-08: -зона creates a place, area, or environment centered on the root: гаме → гаме-зона = game area.
END-09: -ный creates a root-based adjective: креатив → креативный = creative.
END-10: -но creates an adverbial form from a suitable -ный adjective: быстрый-style root forms can become -но.
END-11: -ство creates an abstract state, system, or concept when an abstract noun is needed.
END-12: -макс marks an extreme or maximum version and normally attaches last.
END-13: -мод marks a mode or operating state: хард-мод, софт-мод, дарк-мод.
END-14: -пак creates a bundle/set containing several related root items.
END-15: -дроп creates a release/drop of an item, feature, or content piece.
END-16: -лооп creates a repeated cycle or recurring version of the root.
END-17: -стрим creates a flow/live-stream/context of the root.
END-18: -крафт creates a crafted/buildable version of the root.
END-19: -синк creates synchronization or alignment around the root.
END-20: Only one human-gender ending may appear on a word: *-ьюьж is invalid.
END-21: Gender endings come after all other productive endings: root + builder + suffix + -ью/-ьж.
END-22: Plural marking comes after gender marking when both are required: тичэрьюс / тичэрьжс.
END-23: If a suffix already supplies the human-role meaning, do not duplicate -ер: рид + -инг, not ридингеринг.
END-24: A suffix may only be added when its meaning makes sense; not every root accepts every ending.
END-25: In Casual mode, the final vowel of some long derived forms may be clipped if meaning stays clear.
END-26: Hard mode may remove interior vowels, but never remove -ью or -ьж when gender is explicit.
END-27: Nightmare mode may merge hyphenated compounds, but the root order must remain recoverable.
END-28: When two endings compete, prefer the one that answers the intended question: person, action, object, place, quality, or state.
END-29: Endings are semantic tools, not mandatory inflections; the bare root remains valid.
END-30: New dictionary words should first be entered as a bare root, then optionally list their most useful derived forms.

SELF-DOCUMENTING DICTIONARY RULE
Every new root should be recorded in the same order: English root → ДЖН1 form → part of speech → optional derived forms.
Example: create → крите → verb → критор (creator), критеинг (creating), критека (creation tool), креативный (creative-related).
This keeps the wordbook expandable without turning every new word into a special exception.
ДЖН1 VERSION v6.63.925 — RULE EXPANSION
This release keeps the wordbook format. New rules are integrated as permanent language rules,
not presented as a changelog. v6.63.925 adds a larger productive morphology system, clearer
ending behavior, and a major everyday/root-word expansion.
50 NEW WORD-FORMATION & USAGE RULES
R31. A bare root is always legal unless explicitly marked frozen or slang-only.
R32. The semantic ending is chosen from the intended meaning, not from English spelling.
R33. Human-agent -ер may describe a person of any gender; add -ью or -ьж only when gender matters.
R34. A feminine human form is root + derivational ending + ью; a masculine human form is root + derivational ending + ьж.
R35. -ью and -ьж never change the root itself.
R36. If a root already ends in a visually similar sequence, insert the gender ending intact rather than deleting letters.
R37. -ка creates a concrete tool/object only when the root action can reasonably be performed by an object.
R38. -зона creates a place, scene, environment, or designated area.
R39. -ство creates an abstract concept, collective state, practice, or system.
R40. -ность may be used for a property or quality when -ство would sound too institutional.
R41. -ник creates a person associated with a root, hobby, scene, or recurring activity.
R42. -ист creates a person strongly associated with a field, ideology, craft, or specialty.
R43. -чик creates a small, casual, cute, or informal object/person form when context supports it.
R44. -ик creates a compact or familiar noun; it is stylistic, not mandatory.
R45. -ка and -ник should not be stacked unless the result is a deliberate coined compound.
R46. -ость may be used as a compact abstract-quality ending in Hard mode.
R47. -ный forms descriptive adjectives; -но forms the corresponding manner/adverb when natural.
R48. Comparative meaning uses море before an adjective; superlative meaning uses макс or the -макс builder.
R49. Negative adjective meaning can use ун- before the root or adjective, provided the result remains readable.
R50. Repetition of the final vowel is allowed after derivation and comes after all suffixes.
R51. Emotional lengthening never changes dictionary identity.
R52. A hyphen is preferred when two productive builders would otherwise become visually unreadable.
R53. Compound roots keep English semantic order: modifier first, head second.
R54. A compound may be lexicalized if speakers repeatedly use it for one concept.
R55. Lexicalized compounds are written as one word in Casual and Standard, optionally hyphenated in teaching text.
R56. Personal names remain Latin by default but may receive a ДЖН1 phonetic spelling in creative text.
R57. Brand names, URLs, code, file paths, and identifiers are preserved exactly in Latin unless intentionally stylized.
R58. Numbers remain numeric in technical writing; spoken-number forms are used in ordinary prose.
R59. Time expressions prefer direct English-like ordering: number + time unit.
R60. Dates are ordered day + month + year in ordinary ДЖН1 prose unless the surrounding context is technical.
R61. The plural marker follows the complete lexical word and any explicit gender marker.
R62. A plural gender-marked human form identifies a gendered group only when the speaker intends that distinction.
R63. Mixed-gender groups default to the unmarked plural unless a gender distinction is important.
R64. Pronouns may remain unmarked even when a noun is gender-marked; agreement is optional.
R65. Adjectives do not obligatorily agree with noun gender.
R66. Profession and role nouns can always remain gender-neutral.
R67. Technical roots accept productive endings exactly like everyday roots.
R68. Slang roots can take productive endings only when the resulting meaning is understandable from context.
R69. Frozen abbreviations do not take productive endings unless the abbreviation has become a normal noun.
R70. In Casual mode, a common ending may be omitted when the bare root already communicates the intended role.
R71. In Standard mode, use the ending when it adds information that would otherwise be ambiguous.
R72. In Hard mode, productive endings may be compressed internally but must remain recoverable.
R73. Nightmare mode permits heavier clipping, but semantic suffix order never changes.
R74. Person/agent endings precede gender endings.
R75. Place endings follow the main root or named activity and generally precede mood particles.
R76. Adjective endings precede adverb endings: root + -ный + -но.
R77. Abstract noun endings normally come after the root and before any optional register marker.
R78. One word should not carry two competing aspect meanings unless it is a deliberate lexicalized exception.
R79. Tense/aspect particles remain separate words even when the verb itself has productive derivation.
R80. Negation stays outside derivational morphology: не + derived word.
R81. Question particles remain separate from the derived word.
R82. Emphasis particles же and то follow the lexical phrase they emphasize.
R83. Casual fillers ка and ну remain external to the lexical root.
R84. A newly coined word should be tested in at least one sentence before being treated as stable vocabulary.
R85. A root with multiple English meanings may keep one ДЖН1 form; context selects the intended sense.
R86. If two meanings become consistently confusing, a second root form may be created rather than forcing one form to do everything.
R87. Borrowed international terms may stay visually close to English while still using Cyrillic letters.
R88. Cyrillic spelling should prioritize recognizability over perfect phonetic reconstruction.
R89. The native name of the language is ДЖН1-Language; DXN1-Language remains valid for Latin technical contexts.
R90. The numeral 1 is immutable in the language name and is never rewritten as a word inside the official name.

========================================================================================
ДЖН1-LANGUAGE v6.63.927 — ROOT WORD EXPANSION & MORPHOLOGY UPDATE
========================================================================================

RELEASE STATUS
This edition is a cleaned continuation of v6.63.925. Repeated dictionary headwords from earlier batches were removed during normalization; new additions are checked against the existing headword set and DXN1 spellings.

NEW MORPHOLOGY RULES (WR51–WR100)
========================================================================================
WR51. A bare root is the default dictionary form and carries no derivational meaning until an ending is added.
WR52. Derivational endings attach after the root and after any single productive prefix.
WR53. Gender endings -ью and -ьж are final endings in Standard mode; they never appear before a derivational ending.
WR54. If both derivation and gender are needed, use ROOT + DERIVATION + GENDER.
WR55. Plural marking follows gender marking when gender is explicitly present; otherwise it follows the base or derivational form.
WR56. The ending -ер creates a human agent or habitual doer from an action root.
WR57. The ending -ник creates a person associated with a field, object, habit, or role.
WR58. The ending -ист creates a specialist, practitioner, or strong identity around the root.
WR59. The ending -чик creates a smaller, informal, or task-focused agent/object; tone decides which reading is intended.
WR60. The ending -ик creates a compact noun for an object, unit, or familiar item derived from the root.
WR61. The ending -инг creates an ongoing activity, event, or process and may also function as a gerund-like noun.
WR62. The ending -ед creates a finished result, completed state, or aftermath of the root action.
WR63. The ending -ка creates a concrete tool, device, container, or object used for the root action.
WR64. The ending -зона creates a place, space, or environment associated with the root.
WR65. The ending -ный creates an adjective describing an inherent or characteristic relation to the root.
WR66. The ending -но creates an adverb or manner word derived from an adjective/root.
WR67. The ending -ство creates an abstract system, condition, institution, practice, or collective concept.
WR68. The ending -ность creates an abstract quality or degree of being described by the root.
WR69. The ending -арь creates a keeper, operator, clerk, or role centered on a place/object where context supports it.
WR70. The ending -дом creates a hub, house, center, or dedicated space for the root concept.
WR71. The ending -вейв creates a style, trend, aesthetic, or cultural wave related to the root.
WR72. The ending -мод creates a deliberate mode or configuration of the root concept.
WR73. The ending -макс creates an intensified or maximized version and is incompatible with another maximum-intensity marker on the same root.
WR74. The ending -дроп creates a release, drop, or act of putting something out into circulation.
WR75. The ending -лооп creates a repeat cycle, recurring process, or looped behavior.
WR76. The ending -синк creates an alignment, synchronization, or matching relation.
WR77. The ending -крафт creates a crafted product, build, or making-process.
WR78. The ending -пак creates a bundle, set, collection, or packaged group of the root concept.
WR79. Two productive endings of different semantic families may be chained only when the first ending produces a stable noun-like base.
WR80. If a chained derivation becomes hard to parse in Standard mode, rewrite it as a compound rather than stacking another ending.
WR81. Final orthographic emphasis, including repeated letters, is applied after every derivational and gender ending is attached.
WR82. Hard mode may shorten repeated derivational endings only when the remaining form is still uniquely recoverable.
WR83. A gendered derived noun keeps its lexical meaning while the gender ending changes only the referent's gender.
WR84. -ью marks female/feminine referents; -ьж marks male/masculine referents; no gender ending leaves gender unspecified.
WR85. The gender endings are semantic, not grammatical agreement markers, so unrelated nouns do not receive gender endings automatically.
WR86. In a sentence with explicit gendered occupation or relationship nouns, nearby pronouns may remain unmarked unless contrast is needed.
WR87. If a root already ends in the same sound as a productive ending, keep both only when the resulting boundary remains readable.
WR88. If a boundary becomes visually confusing, insert a soft separator dot · in Nightmare mode or use a hyphen in explanatory text.
WR89. Compounds are written modifier-first: the first root narrows or describes the second root.
WR90. A compound may receive one outer derivational ending if the compound is treated as one lexical unit.
WR91. A compound may receive a gender ending only when the whole compound refers to a person or gendered social role.
WR92. Productive endings do not change the pronunciation of the root unless a defined spelling rule explicitly requires it.
WR93. When a derived word is shortened in Casual mode, preserve its first root syllable and enough of the ending to remain recognizable.
WR94. New technical terms should prefer direct loan roots, while everyday concepts should prefer existing DXN1 roots when available.
WR95. A newly coined word should be entered in the wordbook with its English meaning, DXN1 form, category, and at least one example.
WR96. If two roots would produce identical DXN1 spellings, the newer coinage must use a disambiguating ending, compound, or alternate root.
WR97. Synonyms are allowed, but each synonym should be assigned a register such as neutral, casual, hard, poetic, technical, or slang.
WR98. A borrowed internet term may remain more English-looking in Casual mode but should have a Cyrillic Standard form when one is established.
WR99. Dictionary entries are ordered by semantic category in the wordbook, while actual sentence order remains subject + tense/aspect + verb + object by default.
WR100. When a new ending becomes common enough to be productive, it must be documented with its meaning, attachment position, restrictions, and at least five example words.

WORDBOOK DEDUPLICATION NOTE
========================================================================================
This release uses the first occurrence of each existing dictionary headword and excludes newly generated headwords that were already present. DXN1 spellings are also checked for collisions; collisions are rejected from the new batch rather than silently duplicated.

VERSION: 6.63.926
NATIVE NAME: ДЖН1-Language
LATIN NAME: DXN1-Language


========================================================================================
ENGLISH FOUNDATION & WORD-FORMATION RULES v6.63.927
========================================================================================
WF101. Every canonical English headword may have exactly one primary DXN1 dictionary root.
WF102. Duplicate English headwords are forbidden; alternate senses live under the same entry.
WF103. Inflected forms such as plural, past, gerund, and comparative are normally generated from the root instead of receiving duplicate headword entries.
WF104. A productive ending is appended only after the root is fixed.
WF105. Gender markers -ью (female) and -ьж (male) follow the complete derived word.
WF106. If both gender and plurality are needed, use root + derivation + gender + plural.
WF107. The default unmarked form is neutral/unspecified unless the meaning inherently specifies sex.
WF108. -ер marks a person/agent; it does not automatically mean male.
WF109. -инг marks an action, activity, process, or ongoing practice.
WF110. -ед marks a completed result or resulting state when naturally understood.
WF111. -ка marks a tool, device, or concrete object associated with the root.
WF112. -зона marks a place, area, or environment associated with the root.
WF113. -ный marks a descriptive adjective.
WF114. -но marks a manner/adverbial form.
WF115. -ство marks an abstract state, system, domain, or collective concept.
WF116. -ник may mark a person associated with a field, habit, or thing.
WF117. -чик marks a small tool, small agent, or informal agent when appropriate.
WF118. -ист marks a specialist, practitioner, or follower of an idea.
WF119. -ность marks an abstract property when an adjective root is available.
WF120. English loanwords keep their recognizable root shape even when DXN1 suffixes are attached.
WF121. Cyrillic spelling is the canonical display form; Latin spelling may be retained for URLs, brands, code, and technical identifiers.
WF122. A newly coined root should preserve enough of the English shape that an English reader can guess it.
WF123. Internal vowel compression is permitted only in Hard/Nightmare mode and must not destroy the root.
WF124. A derivational ending cannot be attached twice unless the second attachment creates a clearly different grammatical category.
WF125. Semantic headwords such as light, right, left, watch, match, play, and file keep multiple senses under one English entry.
WF126. Hyphenated English compounds may be stored as one lexical entry when they function as a single concept.
WF127. Ordinary English phrases are not automatically dictionary headwords; fixed expressions belong in the phrasebook.
WF128. Acronyms remain Latin unless a stable spoken form has become an ordinary word.
WF129. Proper names are catalogued separately from the core English headword inventory.
WF130. Regional spellings may map to the same DXN1 root when their meaning is identical.
WF131. British and American variants may share one canonical entry with a variant note.
WF132. Silent English letters may be omitted in the DXN1 spelling when the resulting form is more readable.
WF133. Pronunciation-driven respelling may override strict letter-by-letter transliteration when needed for readability.
WF134. The root remains stable across Casual, Standard, and Hard modes; only presentation may compress.
WF135. Nightmare mode may use symbolic shorthand but the standard form remains the authoritative dictionary form.
WF136. A root ending in a derivational-looking English sequence must not be stripped incorrectly; dictionary roots are atomic unless explicitly derived.
WF137. Gender applies to human or personified referents; ordinary objects remain unmarked.
WF138. Biological sex terms and gendered role nouns may use -ью and -ьж when the distinction is semantically relevant.
WF139. When a word already ends in a gender suffix, do not add another gender suffix.
WF140. When a compound refers to a person, gender marking applies to the final head of the compound.
WF141. Person compounds retain English-order compounding: modifier first, head second.
WF142. Abstract nouns normally do not take gender marking.
WF143. Tool nouns normally do not take gender marking unless personification is intended.
WF144. Place nouns use -зона only when the derived place is a productive concept, not for every geographical proper name.
WF145. Adjectives may be nominalized with -ство when the meaning naturally becomes an abstract concept.
WF146. Adverbs formed with -но modify verbs, adjectives, or whole clauses.
WF147. Agent nouns may take -ью or -ьж after -ер, -ист, or -ник: root+agent+gender.
WF148. A plural marker follows gender when both are present.
WF149. A question particle never becomes part of a dictionary root.
WF150. Tense and aspect particles remain separate words and never become permanent suffixes.
WF151. Negation remains external to the root and does not create a new dictionary entry.
WF152. Productive prefixes remain before the root and before derivational endings.
WF153. A prefix + root + suffix has fixed order: prefix + root + suffix.
WF154. Multiple prefixes require a hyphen and are treated as a compound derivation.
WF155. A lexical root may support several derived families without changing the underlying English headword.
WF156. If a derived form becomes lexicalized with a new meaning, it may be entered as a separate headword only when the English source word itself is distinct.
WF157. Synonyms are allowed; duplicate headwords are not.
WF158. Homographs with unrelated meanings share an English headword entry and receive numbered senses.
WF159. Homophones with different spellings remain separate headwords.
WF160. Abbreviations are stored only when they are common enough to function as words in English usage.
WF161. Number words are lexical entries but numeric forms remain valid outside the lexicon.
WF162. Symbols such as %, $, @, and # are not treated as ordinary roots.
WF163. Punctuation never changes the lexical identity of a word.
WF164. Repeated letters express emotion or emphasis but do not create a new headword.
WF165. Casual contractions are frozen forms unless a standard derivation is explicitly defined.
WF166. Slang roots may be dictionary-valid even when they are informal.
WF167. Offensive words remain lexical entries but are tagged by register.
WF168. Technical terminology may be kept closer to English pronunciation than everyday vocabulary.
WF169. Scientific terms may retain Greek/Latin-looking clusters when that improves recognizability.
WF170. Medical terminology will use a dedicated domain section rather than being mixed into ordinary daily vocabulary.
WF171. Diseases, symptoms, anatomy, treatments, and drug classes should each receive separate domain tags.
WF172. Animal species and plant species are domain entries, not ordinary people/objects categories.
WF173. Chemical elements and compounds use standardized scientific names when necessary.
WF174. A word imported from another language may remain a loanword if English treats it as a normal lexical item.
WF175. Dictionary sorting is by English headword, not by DXN1 spelling.
WF176. Every new entry must pass the duplicate check against all earlier English headwords.
WF177. Every new root should have one clear canonical spelling before Casual/Hard variants are generated.
WF178. Hard forms may omit internal vowels but never the first and last structural consonants when this would make the root ambiguous.
WF179. Casual forms may shorten long roots, but Standard remains canonical.
WF180. Every major domain expansion gets its own heading so specialist vocabulary remains searchable.

MASTER VOCABULARY ROADMAP

CORE ENGLISH: common everyday headwords and function vocabulary.
EXTENDED ENGLISH: less-common but general-purpose headwords.
MEDICINE: diseases, disorders, symptoms, anatomy, treatments, procedures, specialties, drugs.
BIOLOGY: organisms, cells, tissues, genetics, ecology, taxonomy.
CHEMISTRY: elements, compounds, reactions, laboratory vocabulary.
PHYSICS: mechanics, energy, matter, fields, waves, thermodynamics, quantum vocabulary.
MATHEMATICS: arithmetic, algebra, geometry, calculus, statistics, discrete mathematics.
TECHNOLOGY: computing, networking, software, hardware, electronics, cybersecurity, AI.
ENGINEERING: civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, aerospace and industrial terms.
LAW & GOVERNMENT: legal terminology, institutions, rights, procedures and political vocabulary.
FINANCE & ECONOMICS: banking, markets, accounting, investing, commerce and trade.
EDUCATION: school, university, pedagogy, academic research and assessment.
SCIENCE: general scientific vocabulary plus domain-specific terminology.
NATURE: animals, plants, fungi, minerals, weather, geography, geology and astronomy.
CULTURE: art, music, literature, film, theatre, mythology and traditions.
SPORTS: disciplines, positions, equipment, scoring and tactics.
TRANSPORT: vehicles, roads, rail, aviation, shipping and navigation.
MILITARY: ranks, equipment, logistics, strategy and historical terminology.
FOOD: ingredients, cooking, cuisine, dishes, flavors, equipment and restaurant vocabulary.
BODY & DAILY LIFE: clothing, household items, personal care, routines and social interaction.
SLANG & INTERNET: memes, abbreviations, gamer language, texting and modern informal speech.

================================================================================
ДЖН1-LANGUAGE v6.63.928 — LEXICAL ADAPTATION / NON-LITERAL WORD FORMS
================================================================================

Purpose:
DXN1 words do NOT have to remain literal English transliterations. The language
may deliberately reshape common words so that they feel native to DXN1 while
remaining recognizable enough to learn.

LA1. English is the semantic source, not a mandatory spelling source.
LA2. A common word may receive a native DXN1 form that differs substantially
     from English pronunciation.
LA3. New native forms must remain unique: one English headword must map to one
     canonical DXN1 headword in the master dictionary.
LA4. A native form may be shortened, shifted, blended, or rebuilt rather than
     copied letter-for-letter.
LA5. High-frequency words get the strongest permission to become irregular.
LA6. Function words may be highly irregular because they are used constantly.
LA7. Content words normally retain at least one recognizable semantic cue.
LA8. Two English words with similar pronunciation must not automatically receive
     the same DXN1 form.
LA9. If a collision appears, the newer form must be reshaped.
LA10. Native forms take priority over literal transliterations once officially
      entered into the dictionary.
LA11. Casual speech may shorten native forms further.
LA12. Hard mode may compress a native form, but compression must preserve identity.
LA13. Gender suffixes remain -ью (female) and -ьж (male).
LA14. Gender suffixes attach to the canonical DXN1 form, never to the English form.
LA15. Productive suffixes attach after the canonical root.
LA16. A native root may have an irregular derived family if that family is common.
LA17. Compound words may fuse their roots and undergo phonetic smoothing.
LA18. Repeated consonants may collapse when a fused form becomes easier to say.
LA19. Adjacent vowels may merge or change when a compound becomes established.
LA20. A word may acquire a linking consonant in a compound to avoid awkward
      pronunciation.
LA21. English silent letters do not need to survive in DXN1.
LA22. English spelling is never used as the pronunciation authority.
LA23. Stress may move in native DXN1 forms.
LA24. A native form may preserve meaning while abandoning English sound similarity.
LA25. Borrowed international terms may remain closer to their international form.
LA26. Slang is allowed to become more distant from English than formal vocabulary.
LA27. Child/family vocabulary may use especially short native forms.
LA28. Frequent greetings and particles may become lexicalized irregularly.
LA29. Numbers and core pronouns may use irregular forms for speed.
LA30. Native irregularity must be documented in the master wordbook.
LA31. Every irregular form must have a clear English headword reference.
LA32. Synonymous English words may share a DXN1 root only when the meanings are
      intentionally merged; otherwise separate roots are required.
LA33. A DXN1 root should not be created solely by changing one letter from an
      existing DXN1 root if that creates ambiguity.
LA34. Near-homophones are resolved by changing a vowel, consonant cluster, or
      syllable.
LA35. Common words may receive a "native tier" and a "literal tier"; native is
      preferred in normal speech.
LA36. Literal tier forms remain acceptable when the speaker needs transparency.
LA37. Dictionaries list NATIVE first when a native form exists.
LA38. Technical terminology can use a more literal form when precision matters.
LA39. Casual forms may omit unstressed vowels.
LA40. Formal forms may restore vowels that casual speech drops.
LA41. Native forms can be created by analogy with existing DXN1 families.
LA42. Analogy must never create duplicate English headwords.
LA43. A native root can generate verbs, nouns, adjectives and agents through the
      existing productive ending system.
LA44. If a root ends awkwardly before -ью or -ьж, phonetic smoothing is allowed
      but the gender marker remains recognizable.
LA45. Plural marking follows gender marking when both are present.
LA46. A native form can become the base for compounds instead of its English source.
LA47. Compound order remains governed by DXN1 syntax, not English spelling.
LA48. Native forms should favor easy Cyrillic reading.
LA49. The letter X from the Latin name DXN1 is represented by Ж in the native
      language name: ДЖН1.
LA50. "ДЖН1 лэнг" is the canonical native expression for "DXN1 language".
LA51. English words may be grouped into regular, adapted, and irregular classes.
LA52. Regular words follow normal phonetic conversion.
LA53. Adapted words receive controlled sound changes.
LA54. Irregular words are independently lexicalized and must be memorized.
LA55. A word becomes irregular only when it is useful enough to justify the
      exception.
LA56. The adaptation system is productive but not mandatory for every new word.
LA57. New coinages should prefer existing native sound patterns over random spelling.
LA58. Native forms should avoid accidental offensive or confusing forms where
      practical.
LA59. A native form that becomes ambiguous in a sentence may be replaced by its
      transparent/literal form.
LA60. The master dictionary must always preserve the English source meaning even
      when the DXN1 form is no longer phonetically obvious.

================================================================================
ДЖН1-LANGUAGE v6.63.929 — NATIVE WORLD EXPANSION
================================================================================

This edition extends the non-literal/native adaptation system into the natural
world, medicine, anatomy, animals, geology, minerals, science, and geography.

NA1. A domain root may use a native form even when an older literal form exists.
NA2. Native forms are preferred in ordinary speech once officially registered.
NA3. Scientific precision may retain an international form when necessary.
NA4. Every new English headword remains unique in the master dictionary.
NA5. Related meanings may share a root only when the semantic relationship is
    explicitly documented.
NA6. Domain compounds use the normal DXN1 modifier + head order.
NA7. Productive suffixes continue to attach to native roots, not English spellings.
NA8. Gender markers -ью and -ьж remain post-root.
NA9. Plural marking remains after gender marking when both occur.
NA10. Medical, botanical, mineral, and scientific terms may be long in Standard
     mode and compressed in Hard/Nightmare mode.
NA11. International scientific terms may be treated as transparent loan roots.
NA12. A native root that becomes confusing may keep a transparent alias.
NA13. Alias forms do not count as duplicate English headwords.
NA14. A category may contain both general and specialist meanings under one
     headword when the English source word is identical.
NA15. Canonical forms are the preferred dictionary entries; aliases are secondary.

NATIVE DERIVATION EXTENSIONS
================================================================================

NA16. -ер creates an agent from a native verb/root.
NA17. -ник creates a person strongly associated with a root or activity.
NA18. -ка creates a tool, object, or concrete implementation.
NA19. -инг creates an ongoing process or activity.
NA20. -ед creates a completed result/state.
NA21. -зона creates a place, field, or bounded environment.
NA22. -ность creates an abstract quality or condition.
NA23. -ист creates a specialist or adherent.
NA24. -чик creates a small agent, helper, or diminutive object when natural.
NA25. -ный creates an adjective.
NA26. -но creates an adverbial form.
NA27. -ство creates an abstract collective/state concept.
NA28. -ью marks feminine gender on people/role words.
NA29. -ьж marks masculine gender on people/role words.
NA30. Derivational endings are attached to the canonical DXN1 root.
NA31. Gender is added after derivational morphology.
NA32. Plural is added after gender when both are required.
NA33. A tool noun and an agent noun must not share the same canonical ending if
     that would create ambiguity.
NA34. Domain-specific words may introduce documented specialist endings later.
NA35. Native adaptation always comes before suffixing.
NA36. Example: медицина-root → медицинер = medical worker/agent.
NA37. Example: флора-root → флорный = botanical/adjectival.
NA38. Example: минара-root → минер = miner/specialist.
NA39. Example: лава-root → лавка = lava-related object/form, where context permits.
NA40. Example: диза-root → дизер = disease-related agent/specialist only when
     explicitly intended; common medical roles should use established roots such
     as докта, нёрса, сурга, фарма.


TOTAL NEW UNIQUE HEADWORDS THIS EDITION: 431


================================================================================
ДЖН1-LANGUAGE v6.63.930 — LARGE NATIVE VOCABULARY EXPANSION
================================================================================

This edition deliberately shifts more common and specialist vocabulary away from
literal English transcription. The goal is not to hide meaning, but to make
ДЖН1 feel like an independent language with recognizable internal patterns.

NATIVE TIDING RULES
NT1. High-frequency vocabulary may receive a native lexical form even when a
    literal Cyrillic transcription would be understandable.
NT2. Native forms outrank literal forms in Standard speech once registered.
NT3. Literal forms remain legal as transparency forms in technical, teaching,
    quoting, and emergency contexts.
NT4. New native forms should preserve semantic identity, not necessarily sound.
NT5. Native forms may alter vowel quality, consonant clusters, syllable count,
    and endings.
NT6. The canonical form must be unique within the English headword dictionary.
NT7. Two different English headwords may not be merged merely because their
    DXN1 forms sound similar.
NT8. When collision occurs, the newer form takes a phonetic twist.
NT9. Common words may become irregular because frequent speech encourages drift.
NT10. Once an irregular form is established, derivatives are built from the
     irregular DXN1 root.
NT11. Native forms can be shorter than their English source.
NT12. Native forms can also be longer when an ending improves readability.
NT13. Final -а/-о/-е/-и can be used to create a smoother noun shape.
NT14. Final -а may become a common everyday noun ending.
NT15. Final -о may be favored for concrete objects and compact terms.
NT16. Final -и may be favored for quick conversational vocabulary.
NT17. Final -ма/-на/-са may mark conceptual or process-heavy vocabulary.
NT18. Final -ка may remain a productive concrete-object ending.
NT19. Final -ер/-ник/-ист remain productive human-agent endings.
NT20. -ью and -ьж remain the only canonical explicit feminine/masculine gender
     endings introduced in the current system.
NT21. Native adaptation happens before productive derivation.
NT22. Gender happens after derivation.
NT23. Plural happens after gender.
NT24. Compounds may fuse and smooth one or both roots.
NT25. A compound may have a special lexicalized form if it becomes common.
NT26. Lexicalized compounds cannot be mistaken for ordinary productive compounds.
NT27. Scientific words may keep recognizable international roots while still
     undergoing native smoothing.
NT28. Diseases may use shorter native roots in ordinary conversation and fuller
     transparent forms in medical writing.
NT29. Plant names may favor natural endings; mineral names may favor crisp consonants.
NT30. Animal names may favor short, distinctive two-syllable forms.
NT31. Abstract nouns may favor -ма, -на, -ство, or -ность.
NT32. Adjectives can be formed from native roots with -ный.
NT33. Adverbs can be formed with -но where needed.
NT34. Action/process nouns use -инг where a progressive sense is intended.
NT35. Finished-result nouns use -ед where the result matters.
NT36. Place/field nouns use -зона.
NT37. A root can have several derivations, but each must remain semantically
     distinct.
NT38. A derivation that becomes ambiguous must be lexicalized separately.
NT39. Hard mode may reduce vowels, but never deletes gender markers or tense/aspect.
NT40. Nightmare mode may additionally fuse common particles when the clause remains
     parseable.
NT41. Casual forms can become frozen slang and then develop their own dictionary entry.
NT42. Frozen slang cannot automatically inherit every productive suffix.
NT43. Technical abbreviations stay in Latin/Cyrillic mixed form when the domain
     convention requires it.
NT44. Names and brands are not forced through native adaptation.
NT45. Geographic names can keep internationally recognizable forms.
NT46. Medical drug names may stay close to the international scientific form.
NT47. Newly invented native words should be pronounceable by a Cyrillic reader.
NT48. Avoid more than three difficult consonants in a row in Standard mode.
NT49. A difficult cluster may be repaired with a linking vowel.
NT50. A native word can become more distant from English over time if speakers
     adopt it and its meaning remains stable.
NT51. The language officially recognizes REGULAR, ADAPTED, and IRREGULAR word classes.
NT52. REGULAR = normal English-root adaptation.
NT53. ADAPTED = controlled sound/shape change.
NT54. IRREGULAR = independently lexicalized native form.
NT55. Dictionary entries should identify the class whenever an unusual form is used.
NT56. One English headword still gets one canonical master entry.
NT57. Synonyms can be listed under a single English headword without creating
     duplicate headwords.
NT58. Polysemy is represented by multiple meanings beneath the same headword.
NT59. Homographs with unrelated meanings may receive numbered senses rather than
     duplicate English keys.
NT60. The aim is recognizable meaning plus genuine ДЖН1 identity, not perfect
     transliteration.

================================================================================
CANONICAL NATIVE-TWIST SHOWCASE
================================================================================

These are intentional non-literal forms demonstrating the evolved character of
ДЖН1. They are examples of the rule system, not English spelling errors.

computer → компа
language → лэнго
medicine → медика
disease → диза
flower → флора
mineral → минара
forest → фора
animal → анима
school → скула
teacher → тича
student → студо
friend → френо
family → фамо
question → квеста
answer → анса
problem → проба
important → импа
beautiful → бьюта
tomorrow → тумо
yesterday → йеста

NT61. A showcase native form may be promoted to canonical status after repeated
     usage, but only one canonical English headword entry is kept.
NT62. When a native twist exists, speakers may still use the transparent form to
     teach beginners without changing the dictionary headword.
NT63. Native twists are strongest in Casual and Standard; Hard compresses them
     rather than reverting them to English.
NT64. A word should feel like it belongs to ДЖН1 before it is considered fully
     native, even if its English source remains obvious.
NT65. Future domain expansions should prefer native adaptation first, then add
     international scientific aliases only when useful.


================================================================================
ДЖН1-LANGUAGE v6.63.931 — LARGE NATIVE ENGLISH EXPANSION
================================================================================
NT66. The English headword is the semantic key; the DXN1 form is the native realization.
NT67. Common English morphology may disappear completely in a native form.
NT68. -tion/-sion families may collapse into -ша/-жа or another lexicalized ending.
NT69. -ment/-ship/-hood/-dom may collapse toward -ма.
NT70. -ness/-ity may collapse toward -на.
NT71. -able/-ible may collapse toward -аба/-иба.
NT72. -ous/-ious may collapse toward -оса.
NT73. -ive/-ative may collapse toward -ива.
NT74. Agent endings -er/-or are not preserved literally by default.
NT75. Frequent roots may lose a syllable when identity remains clear in context.
NT76. Infrequent roots should remain more transparent than high-frequency roots.
NT77. Native forms may shift vowel classes to match established DXN1 sound patterns.
NT78. Native forms may insert linking vowels between difficult consonant clusters.
NT79. Native forms may simplify repeated consonants.
NT80. Native adaptation happens before productive suffixing.
NT81. Gender is appended after productive derivation.
NT82. Plural is appended after gender when both are present.
NT83. Native forms are preferred in Standard speech once registered.
NT84. Literal forms remain legal for teaching, quoting, and precision.
NT85. Scientific terminology may retain transparent aliases.
NT86. Medical terminology may use short native roots in ordinary speech.
NT87. Plant names may favor open syllables.
NT88. Animal names should remain distinct enough for conversation.
NT89. Mineral names may favor compact consonant shapes.
NT90. Abstract vocabulary may favor -ма, -на, -ство, or -ность.
NT91. One English headword gets one canonical master entry.
NT92. Synonyms stay under their own English keys but can share a semantic family.
NT93. Polysemous meanings remain beneath one English headword.
NT94. New native collisions are repaired by a documented phonetic twist.
NT95. High-frequency irregular forms may become conventional.
NT96. Derived forms use the conventional native root, not English spelling.
NT97. REGULAR, ADAPTED, and IRREGULAR remain distinct lexical classes.
NT98. REGULAR follows ordinary sound mapping.
NT99. ADAPTED intentionally reshapes sound/structure while keeping meaning.
NT100. IRREGULAR is independently lexicalized and must be learned as a root.
NT101. The aim is semantic recognizability plus genuine ДЖН1 identity.
